payload.content:
## User Guide[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#user-guide)

The User Guide covers all of pandas by topic area. Each of the subsections introduces a topic (such as “working with missing data”), and discusses how pandas approaches the problem, with many examples throughout.

Users brand-new to pandas should start with [10 minutes to pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/10min.html#min).

For a high level summary of the pandas fundamentals, see [Intro to data structures](https://pandas.pydata.org/dsintro.html#dsintro) and [Essential basic functionality](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics).

Further information on any specific method can be obtained in the
[API reference](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/index.html#api).

payload.content:
## How to read these guides[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#how-to-read-these-guides)

In these guides you will see input code inside code blocks such as:

```
import pandas as pd
pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3]})
```
or:

```
In [1]: import pandas as pd
In [2]: pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3]})
Out[2]: 
   A
0  1
1  2
2  3
```
The first block is a standard Python input, while in the second the `In [1]:`
indicates the input is inside a [notebook](https://jupyter.org). In Jupyter Notebooks the last line is printed and plots are shown inline.

For example:

```
In [3]: a = 1
In [4]: a
Out[4]: 1
```
is equivalent to:

```
a = 1
print(a)
```

**Date**: Oct 22, 2026 **Version**: 3.1.0

**Download documentation**: [Zipped HTML](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas.zip)

[`pandas`](https://pandas.pydata.org#module-pandas) is an open source, BSD-licensed library providing high-performance,
easy-to-use data structures and data analysis tools for the [Python](https://www.python.org/)
programming language.

New to *pandas*? Check out the getting started guides. They contain an
introduction to *pandas’* main concepts and links to additional tutorials.

The user guide provides in-depth information on the key concepts of pandas with useful background information and explanation.

The reference guide contains a detailed description of the pandas API. The reference describes how the methods work and which parameters can be used. It assumes that you have an understanding of the key concepts.

Saw a typo in the documentation? Want to improve existing functionalities? The contributing guidelines will guide you through the process of improving pandas.

payload.content:
## Intro to pandas[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-pandas)

When working with tabular data, such as data stored in spreadsheets or databases, pandas is the right tool for you. pandas will help you
to explore, clean, and process your data. In pandas, a data table is called a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame).

pandas supports the integration with many file formats or data sources out of the box (csv, excel, sql, json, parquet,…). The ability to import data from each of these
data sources is provided by functions with the prefix, `read_*`. Similarly, the `to_*` methods are used to store data.

Selecting or filtering specific rows and/or columns? Filtering the data on a particular condition? Methods for slicing, selecting, and extracting the data you need are available in pandas.

pandas provides plotting for your data right out of the box with the power of Matplotlib. Simply pick the plot type (scatter, bar, boxplot,…) corresponding to your data.

There’s no need to loop over all rows of your data table to do calculations. Column data manipulations work elementwise in pandas.
Adding a column to a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) based on existing data in other columns is straightforward.

Basic statistics (mean, median, min, max, counts…) are easily calculable across data frames. These, or even custom aggregations, can be applied on the entire data set, a sliding window of the data, or grouped by categories. The latter is also known as the split-apply-combine approach.

payload.content:
## Coming from…[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#coming-from)

Are you familiar with other software for manipulating tabular data? Learn the pandas-equivalent operations compared to software you already know:

Already familiar with `SELECT`, `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, etc.?
Many SQL manipulations have equivalents in pandas.

[SAS](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAS_(software)>), the statistical software suite,
uses the `data set` structure, which closely corresponds pandas’ `DataFrame`.
Also SAS vectorized operations such as filtering or string processing operations
have similar functions in pandas.

payload.content:
## API reference[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#api-reference)

This page gives an overview of all public pandas objects, functions and
methods. All classes and functions exposed in `pandas.*` namespace are public.

The following subpackages are public.

- `pandas.errors`: Custom exception and warnings classes that are raised by pandas.
- `pandas.plotting`: Plotting public API.
- `pandas.testing`: Functions that are useful for writing tests involving pandas objects.
- `pandas.api.extensions`: Functions and classes for extending pandas objects.
- `pandas.api.indexers`: Functions and classes for rolling window indexers.
- `pandas.api.interchange`: DataFrame interchange protocol.
- `pandas.api.types`: Datatype classes and functions.
- `pandas.api.typing`: Classes that may be necessary for type-hinting.
These are classes that are encountered as intermediate results but should not be instantiated
directly by users. These classes are not to be confused with classes from the [pandas-stubs](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas-stubs) package
which has classes in addition to those that occur in pandas for type-hinting.

In addition, public functions in `pandas.io`, `pandas.tseries`, `pandas.util` submodules
are explicitly mentioned in the documentation. Further APIs in these modules are not guaranteed
to be stable.

Warning

The `pandas.core`, `pandas.compat` top-level modules are PRIVATE. Stable functionality in such modules is not guaranteed.

payload.content:
## Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures)

We’ll start with a quick, non-comprehensive overview of the fundamental data structures in pandas to get you started. The fundamental behavior about data types, indexing, axis labeling, and alignment apply across all of the objects. To get started, import NumPy and load pandas into your namespace:

```
In [1]: import numpy as np
In [2]: import pandas as pd
```
Fundamentally, **data alignment is intrinsic**. The link
between labels and data will not be broken unless done so explicitly by you.

We’ll give a brief intro to the data structures, then consider all of the broad categories of functionality and methods in separate sections.

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > Series[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series)
payload.content:
## Series[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series)

[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) is a one-dimensional labeled array capable of holding any data
type (integers, strings, floating point numbers, Python objects, etc.). The axis
labels are collectively referred to as the **index**. The basic method to create a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) is to call:

```
s = pd.Series(data, index=index)
```
Here, `data` can be many different things:

- a Python dict
- an ndarray
- a scalar value (like 5)

The passed **index** is a list of axis labels. The constructor’s behavior
depends on **data**’s type:

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From ndarray[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-ndarray)
payload.content:
## From ndarray[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-ndarray)

If `data` is an ndarray, **index** must be the same length as **data**. If no
index is passed, one will be created having values `[0, ..., len(data) - 1]`.

```
In [3]: s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(5), index=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])
In [4]: s
Out[4]: 
a    0.469112
b   -0.282863
c   -1.509059
d   -1.135632
e    1.212112
dtype: float64
In [5]: s.index
Out[5]: Index(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'], dtype='str')
In [6]: pd.Series(np.random.randn(5))
Out[6]: 
0   -0.173215
1    0.119209
2   -1.044236
3   -0.861849
4   -2.104569
dtype: float64
```
Note

pandas supports non-unique index values. If an operation that does not support duplicate index values is attempted, an exception will be raised at that time.

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From dict[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-dict)
payload.content:
## From dict[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-dict)

[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) can be instantiated from dicts:

```
In [7]: d = {"b": 1, "a": 0, "c": 2}
In [8]: pd.Series(d)
Out[8]: 
b    1
a    0
c    2
dtype: int64
```
If an index is passed, the values in data corresponding to the labels in the index will be pulled out.

```
In [9]: d = {"a": 0.0, "b": 1.0, "c": 2.0}
In [10]: pd.Series(d)
Out[10]: 
a    0.0
b    1.0
c    2.0
dtype: float64
In [11]: pd.Series(d, index=["b", "c", "d", "a"])
Out[11]: 
b    1.0
c    2.0
d    NaN
a    0.0
dtype: float64
```
Note

NaN (not a number) is the standard missing data marker used in pandas.

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From scalar value[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-scalar-value)
payload.content:
## From scalar value[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-scalar-value)

If `data` is a scalar value, the value will be repeated to match
the length of **index**.  If the **index** is not provided, it defaults
to `RangeIndex(1)`.

```
In [12]: pd.Series(5.0, index=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])
Out[12]: 
a    5.0
b    5.0
c    5.0
d    5.0
e    5.0
dtype: float64
```

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > Series is ndarray-like[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series-is-ndarray-like)
payload.content:
## Series is ndarray-like[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series-is-ndarray-like)

[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) acts very similarly to a [`numpy.ndarray`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html#numpy.ndarray) and is a valid argument to most NumPy functions.
However, operations such as slicing will also slice the index.

```
In [13]: s.iloc[0]
Out[13]: np.float64(0.4691122999071863)
In [14]: s.iloc[:3]
Out[14]: 
a    0.469112
b   -0.282863
c   -1.509059
dtype: float64
In [15]: s[s > s.median()]
Out[15]: 
a    0.469112
e    1.212112
dtype: float64
In [16]: s.iloc[[4, 3, 1]]
Out[16]: 
e    1.212112
d   -1.135632
b   -0.282863
dtype: float64
In [17]: np.exp(s)
Out[17]: 
a    1.598575
b    0.753623
c    0.221118
d    0.321219
e    3.360575
dtype: float64
```
Like a NumPy array, a pandas [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) has a single [`dtype`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.dtype.html#pandas.Series.dtype).

```
In [18]: s.dtype
Out[18]: dtype('float64')
```
This is often a NumPy dtype. However, pandas and 3rd-party libraries
extend NumPy’s type system in a few places, in which case the dtype would
be an [`ExtensionDtype`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionDtype.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionDtype). Some examples within
pandas are [Categorical data](https://pandas.pydata.org/categorical.html#categorical) and [Nullable integer data type](https://pandas.pydata.org/integer_na.html#integer-na). See [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics-dtypes)
for more.

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > Series is ndarray-like[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series-is-ndarray-like)
payload.content:
pandas are [Categorical data](https://pandas.pydata.org/categorical.html#categorical) and [Nullable integer data type](https://pandas.pydata.org/integer_na.html#integer-na). See [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics-dtypes)
for more.

If you need the actual array backing a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series), use [`Series.array`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.array.html#pandas.Series.array).

```
In [19]: s.array
Out[19]: 
<NumpyExtensionArray>
[ 0.4691122999071863, -0.2828633443286633, -1.5090585031735124,
 -1.1356323710171934,  1.2121120250208506]
Length: 5, dtype: float64
```
Accessing the array can be useful when you need to do some operation without the
index (to disable [automatic alignment](https://pandas.pydata.org#dsintro-alignment), for example).

[`Series.array`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.array.html#pandas.Series.array) will always be an [`ExtensionArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray).
Briefly, an ExtensionArray is a thin wrapper around one or more *concrete* arrays like a
[`numpy.ndarray`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html#numpy.ndarray). pandas knows how to take an [`ExtensionArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray) and
store it in a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) or a column of a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame).
See [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics-dtypes) for more.

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > Series is ndarray-like[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series-is-ndarray-like)
payload.content:
See [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics-dtypes) for more.

While [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) is ndarray-like, if you need an *actual* ndarray, then use
[`Series.to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.to_numpy.html#pandas.Series.to_numpy).

```
In [20]: s.to_numpy()
Out[20]: array([ 0.4691, -0.2829, -1.5091, -1.1356,  1.2121])
```
Even if the [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) is backed by a [`ExtensionArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray),
[`Series.to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.to_numpy.html#pandas.Series.to_numpy) will return a NumPy ndarray.

payload.content:
## Series is dict-like[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series-is-dict-like)

A [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) is also like a fixed-size dict in that you can get and set values by index
label:

```
In [21]: s["a"]
Out[21]: np.float64(0.4691122999071863)
In [22]: s["e"] = 12.0
In [23]: s
Out[23]: 
a     0.469112
b    -0.282863
c    -1.509059
d    -1.135632
e    12.000000
dtype: float64
In [24]: "e" in s
Out[24]: True
In [25]: "f" in s
Out[25]: False

payload.content:
## Vectorized operations and label alignment with Series[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#vectorized-operations-and-label-alignment-with-series)

When working with raw NumPy arrays, looping through value-by-value is usually
not necessary. The same is true when working with [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) in pandas.
[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) can also be passed into most NumPy methods expecting an ndarray.

```
In [29]: s + s
Out[29]: 
a     0.938225
b    -0.565727
c    -3.018117
d    -2.271265
e    24.000000
dtype: float64
In [30]: s * 2
Out[30]: 
a     0.938225
b    -0.565727
c    -3.018117
d    -2.271265
e    24.000000
dtype: float64
In [31]: np.exp(s)
Out[31]: 
a         1.598575
b         0.753623
c         0.221118
d         0.321219
e    162754.791419
dtype: float64
```
A key difference between [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) and ndarray is that operations between [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series)
automatically align the data based on label. Thus, you can write computations
without giving consideration to whether the [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) involved have the same
labels.

```
In [32]: s.iloc[1:] + s.iloc[:-1]
Out[32]: 
a         NaN
b   -0.565727
c   -3.018117
d   -2.271265
e         NaN
dtype: float64
```
The result of an operation between unaligned [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) will have the **union** of

payload.content:
a         NaN
b   -0.565727
c   -3.018117
d   -2.271265
e         NaN
dtype: float64
```
The result of an operation between unaligned [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) will have the **union** of
the indexes involved. If a label is not found in one [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) or the other, the
result will be marked as missing `NaN`. Being able to write code without doing
any explicit data alignment grants immense freedom and flexibility in
interactive data analysis and research. The integrated data alignment features
of the pandas data structures set pandas apart from the majority of related
tools for working with labeled data.

Note

In general, we chose to make the default result of operations between
differently indexed objects yield the **union** of the indexes in order to
avoid loss of information. Having an index label, though the data is
missing, is typically important information as part of a computation. You
of course have the option of dropping labels with missing data via the
**dropna** function.

payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > Name attribute[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#name-attribute)
payload.content:
## Name attribute[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#name-attribute)

[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) also has a `name` attribute:

```
In [33]: s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(5), name="something")
In [34]: s
Out[34]: 
0   -0.494929
1    1.071804
2    0.721555
3   -0.706771
4   -1.039575
Name: something, dtype: float64
In [35]: s.name
Out[35]: 'something'
```
The `Series``name` can be assigned automatically in many cases, in particular,
when selecting a single column from a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame), the `name` will be assigned
the column label.

You can rename a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) with the [`pandas.Series.rename()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.rename.html#pandas.Series.rename) method.

```
In [36]: s2 = s.rename("different")
In [37]: s2.name
Out[37]: 'different'
```
Note that `s` and `s2` refer to different objects.

payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > DataFrame[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#dataframe)
payload.content:
## DataFrame[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#dataframe)

[`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) is a 2-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of
potentially different types. You can think of it like a spreadsheet or SQL
table, or a dict of Series objects. It is generally the most commonly used
pandas object. Like Series, DataFrame accepts many different kinds of input:

- Dict of 1D ndarrays, lists, dicts, or `Series`
- 2-D numpy.ndarray
- [Structured or record](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.rec.html) ndarray
- A `Series`
- Another `DataFrame`

Along with the data, you can optionally pass **index** (row labels) and
**columns** (column labels) arguments. If you pass an index and / or columns,
you are guaranteeing the index and / or columns of the resulting
DataFrame. Thus, a dict of Series plus a specific index will discard all data
not matching up to the passed index.

If axis labels are not passed, they will be constructed from the input data based on common sense rules.

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From dict of Series or dicts[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-dict-of-series-or-dicts)
payload.content:
## From dict of Series or dicts[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-dict-of-series-or-dicts)

The resulting **index** will be the **union** of the indexes of the various
Series. If there are any nested dicts, these will first be converted to
Series. If no columns are passed, the columns will be the ordered list of dict
keys.

```
In [38]: d = {
   ....:     "one": pd.Series([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], index=["a", "b", "c"]),
   ....:     "two": pd.Series([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], index=["a", "b", "c", "d"]),
   ....: }
   ....: 
In [39]: df = pd.DataFrame(d)
In [40]: df
Out[40]: 
   one  two
a  1.0  1.0
b  2.0  2.0
c  3.0  3.0
d  NaN  4.0
In [41]: pd.DataFrame(d, index=["d", "b", "a"])
Out[41]: 
   one  two
d  NaN  4.0
b  2.0  2.0
a  1.0  1.0
In [42]: pd.DataFrame(d, index=["d", "b", "a"], columns=["two", "three"])
Out[42]: 
   two three
d  4.0   NaN
b  2.0   NaN
a  1.0   NaN
```
The row and column labels can be accessed respectively by accessing the
**index** and **columns** attributes:

Note

When a particular set of columns is passed along with a dict of data, the passed columns override the keys in the dict.

```
In [43]: df.index
Out[43]: Index(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], dtype='str')
In [44]: df.columns
Out[44]: Index(['one', 'two'], dtype='str')
```

payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From dict of ndarrays / lists[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-dict-of-ndarrays-lists)
payload.content:
## From dict of ndarrays / lists[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-dict-of-ndarrays-lists)

All ndarrays must share the same length. If an index is passed, it must
also be the same length as the arrays. If no index is passed, the
result will be `range(n)`, where `n` is the array length.

```
In [45]: d = {"one": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], "two": [4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0]}
In [46]: pd.DataFrame(d)
Out[46]: 
   one  two
0  1.0  4.0
1  2.0  3.0
2  3.0  2.0
3  4.0  1.0
In [47]: pd.DataFrame(d, index=["a", "b", "c", "d"])
Out[47]: 
   one  two
a  1.0  4.0
b  2.0  3.0
c  3.0  2.0
d  4.0  1.0
```

payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From structured or record array[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-structured-or-record-array)
payload.content:
## From structured or record array[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-structured-or-record-array)

This case is handled identically to a dict of arrays.

```
In [48]: data = np.zeros((2,), dtype=[("A", "i4"), ("B", "f4"), ("C", "S10")])
In [49]: data[:] = [(1, 2.0, "Hello"), (2, 3.0, "World")]
In [50]: pd.DataFrame(data)
Out[50]: 
   A    B         C
0  1  2.0  b'Hello'
1  2  3.0  b'World'
In [51]: pd.DataFrame(data, index=["first", "second"])
Out[51]: 
        A    B         C
first   1  2.0  b'Hello'
second  2  3.0  b'World'
In [52]: pd.DataFrame(data, columns=["C", "A", "B"])
Out[52]: 
          C  A    B
0  b'Hello'  1  2.0
1  b'World'  2  3.0
```
Note

DataFrame is not intended to work exactly like a 2-dimensional NumPy ndarray.

In [53]: data2 = [{"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 5, "b": 10, "c": 20}]

## From a dict of tuples[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-a-dict-of-tuples)

You can automatically create a MultiIndexed frame by passing a tuples dictionary.

```
In [57]: pd.DataFrame(
   ....:     {
   ....:         ("a", "b"): {("A", "B"): 1, ("A", "C"): 2},
   ....:         ("a", "a"): {("A", "C"): 3, ("A", "B"): 4},
   ....:         ("a", "c"): {("A", "B"): 5, ("A", "C"): 6},
   ....:         ("b", "a"): {("A", "C"): 7, ("A", "B"): 8},
   ....:         ("b", "b"): {("A", "D"): 9, ("A", "B"): 10},
   ....:     }
   ....: )
   ....: 
Out[57]: 
       a              b      
       b    a    c    a     b
A B  1.0  4.0  5.0  8.0  10.0
  C  2.0  3.0  6.0  7.0   NaN
  D  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN   9.0
```

payload.content:
## From a Series[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-a-series)

The result will be a DataFrame with the same index as the input Series, and with one column whose name is the original name of the Series (only if no other column name provided).

```
In [58]: ser = pd.Series(range(3), index=list("abc"), name="ser")
In [59]: pd.DataFrame(ser)
Out[59]: 
   ser
a    0
b    1
c    2
```

payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From a list of namedtuples[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-a-list-of-namedtuples)
payload.content:
## From a list of namedtuples[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-a-list-of-namedtuples)

The field names of the first `namedtuple` in the list determine the columns
of the [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame). The remaining namedtuples (or tuples) are simply unpacked
and their values are fed into the rows of the [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame), and should all
have the same length as the first `namedtuple`. Passing entries of differing
lengths is deprecated.

```
In [60]: from collections import namedtuple
In [61]: Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")
In [62]: pd.DataFrame([Point(0, 0), Point(0, 3), (2, 3)])
Out[62]: 
   x  y
0  0  0
1  0  3
2  2  3
```

payload.title: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > From a list of dataclasses[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-a-list-of-dataclasses)
payload.content:
## From a list of dataclasses[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#from-a-list-of-dataclasses)

Data Classes as introduced in [PEP557](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0557),
can be passed into the DataFrame constructor.
Passing a list of dataclasses is equivalent to passing a list of dictionaries.

Please be aware, that all values in the list should be dataclasses, mixing
types in the list would result in a `TypeError`.

```
In [63]: from dataclasses import make_dataclass
In [64]: Point = make_dataclass("Point", [("x", int), ("y", int)])
In [65]: pd.DataFrame([Point(0, 0), Point(0, 3), Point(2, 3)])
Out[65]: 
   x  y
0  0  0
1  0  3
2  2  3
```
**Missing data**

To construct a DataFrame with missing data, we use `np.nan` to
represent missing values. Alternatively, you may pass a `numpy.MaskedArray`
as the data argument to the DataFrame constructor, and its masked entries will
be considered missing. See [Missing data](https://pandas.pydata.org/missing_data.html#missing-data) for more.
Note that masked arrays with a structured dtype are not supported;
constructing a DataFrame from one raises an error.

payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > Alternate constructors[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#alternate-constructors)
payload.content:
## Alternate constructors[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#alternate-constructors)

**DataFrame.from\_dict**

[`DataFrame.from_dict()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.from_dict.html#pandas.DataFrame.from_dict) takes a dict of dicts or a dict of array-like sequences
and returns a DataFrame. It operates like the [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) constructor except
for the `orient` parameter which is `'columns'` by default, but which can be
set to `'index'` in order to use the dict keys as row labels.

```
In [66]: pd.DataFrame.from_dict(dict([("A", [1, 2, 3]), ("B", [4, 5, 6])]))
Out[66]: 
   A  B
0  1  4
1  2  5
2  3  6
```
If you pass `orient='index'`, the keys will be the row labels. In this
case, you can also pass the desired column names:

```
In [67]: pd.DataFrame.from_dict(
   ....:     dict([("A", [1, 2, 3]), ("B", [4, 5, 6])]),
   ....:     orient="index",
   ....:     columns=["one", "two", "three"],
   ....: )
   ....: 
Out[67]: 
   one  two  three
A    1    2      3
B    4    5      6
```
**DataFrame.from\_records**

[`DataFrame.from_records()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.from_records.html#pandas.DataFrame.from_records) takes a list of tuples or an ndarray with structured
dtype. It works analogously to the normal [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) constructor, except that
the resulting DataFrame index may be a specific field of the structured
dtype.

```
In [68]: data
Out[68]: 
array([(1, 2., b'Hello'), (2, 3., b'World')],
      dtype=[('A', '<i4'), ('B', '<f4'), ('C', 'S10')])
In [69]: pd.DataFrame.from_records(data, index="C")
Out[69]: 
          A    B
C               
b'Hello'  1  2.0

payload.breadcrumb: Intro to data structures — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Intro to data structures[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#intro-to-data-structures) > Column selection, addition, deletion[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#column-selection-addition-deletion)
payload.content:
## Column selection, addition, deletion[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#column-selection-addition-deletion)

You can treat a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) semantically like a dict of like-indexed [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series)
objects. Getting, setting, and deleting columns works with the same syntax as
the analogous dict operations:

```
In [70]: df["one"]
Out[70]: 
a    1.0
b    2.0
c    3.0
d    NaN
Name: one, dtype: float64
In [71]: df["three"] = df["one"] * df["two"]
In [72]: df["flag"] = df["one"] > 2
In [73]: df
Out[73]: 
   one  two  three   flag
a  1.0  1.0    1.0  False
b  2.0  2.0    4.0  False
c  3.0  3.0    9.0   True
d  NaN  4.0    NaN  False
```
Columns can be deleted or popped like with a dict:

```
In [74]: del df["two"]
In [75]: three = df.pop("three")
In [76]: df
Out[76]: 
   one   flag
a  1.0  False
b  2.0  False
c  3.0   True
d  NaN  False
```
When inserting a scalar value, it will naturally be propagated to fill the column:

```
In [77]: df["foo"] = "bar"
In [78]: df
Out[78]: 
   one   flag  foo
a  1.0  False  bar
b  2.0  False  bar
c  3.0   True  bar
d  NaN  False  bar
```
When inserting a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) that does not have the same index as the [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame), it
will be conformed to the DataFrame’s index:

```
In [79]: df["one_trunc"] = df["one"][:2]
In [80]: df
Out[80]: 
   one   flag  foo  one_trunc
a  1.0  False  bar        1.0
b  2.0  False  bar        2.0
c  3.0   True  bar        NaN
d  NaN  False  bar        NaN
```

## Assigning new columns in method chains[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#assigning-new-columns-in-method-chains)

Inspired by [dplyr’s](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html)
`mutate` verb, DataFrame has an [`assign()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.assign.html#pandas.DataFrame.assign)
method that allows you to easily create new columns that are potentially
derived from existing columns.

```
In [83]: iris = pd.read_csv("data/iris.data")
In [84]: iris.head()
Out[84]: 
   SepalLength  SepalWidth  PetalLength  PetalWidth         Name
0          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  Iris-setosa
1          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  Iris-setosa
2          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  Iris-setosa
3          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2  Iris-setosa
4          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2  Iris-setosa
In [85]: iris.assign(sepal_ratio=iris["SepalWidth"] / iris["SepalLength"]).head()
Out[85]: 
   SepalLength  SepalWidth  PetalLength  PetalWidth         Name  sepal_ratio
0          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  Iris-setosa     0.686275
1          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  Iris-setosa     0.612245
2          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  Iris-setosa     0.680851
3          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2  Iris-setosa     0.673913
4          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2  Iris-setosa     0.720000
```
In the example above, we inserted a precomputed value. We can also pass in a function of one argument to be evaluated on the DataFrame being assigned to.

```
In [86]: iris.assign(sepal_ratio=lambda x: (x["SepalWidth"] / x["SepalLength"])).head()
Out[86]: 
   SepalLength  SepalWidth  PetalLength  PetalWidth         Name  sepal_ratio

we can limit the DataFrame to just those observations with a Sepal Length

Since a function is passed in, the function is computed on the DataFrame

and then the ratio calculations. This is an example where we didn’t
have a reference to the *filtered* DataFrame available.

The function signature for [`assign()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.assign.html#pandas.DataFrame.assign) is simply `**kwargs`. The keys
are the column names for the new fields, and the values are either a value
to be inserted (for example, a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) or NumPy array), or a function
of one argument to be called on the [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame). A *copy* of the original
[`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) is returned, with the new values inserted.

The order of `**kwargs` is preserved. This allows
for *dependent* assignment, where an expression later in `**kwargs` can refer

The order of `**kwargs` is preserved. This allows
for *dependent* assignment, where an expression later in `**kwargs` can refer
to a column created earlier in the same [`assign()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.assign.html#pandas.DataFrame.assign).

```
In [89]: dfa = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [4, 5, 6]})
In [90]: dfa.assign(C=lambda x: x["A"] + x["B"], D=lambda x: x["A"] + x["C"])
Out[90]: 
   A  B  C   D
0  1  4  5   6
1  2  5  7   9
2  3  6  9  12
```
In the second expression, `x['C']` will refer to the newly created column,
that’s equal to `dfa['A'] + dfa['B']`.

payload.content:
## Selecting columns in method chains[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selecting-columns-in-method-chains)

Similar to selecting with `[]`, [`DataFrame.select()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.select.html#pandas.DataFrame.select) returns a DataFrame
with the specified columns, but as a method it composes naturally in chains.
Columns can be given either as individual arguments or as a single list:

```
In [91]: dfa.select("B", "A")
Out[91]: 
   B  A
0  4  1
1  5  2
2  6  3
In [92]: dfa.select(["B", "A"])
Out[92]: 
   B  A
0  4  1
1  5  2
2  6  3
```
Columns can also be computed via [`pandas.col()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.col.html#pandas.col) expressions, or callables
passed as keyword arguments. A positional expression keeps the name of the
underlying column, while a keyword argument names the resulting column:

```
In [93]: dfa.select("A", pd.col("B") * 2, C=pd.col("A") + pd.col("B"))
Out[93]: 
   A   B   C
0  1   8   9
1  2  10  12
2  3  12  15
```
As with [`assign()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.assign.html#pandas.DataFrame.assign), later arguments can refer to
columns computed earlier in the same call, but the result contains only the
requested columns:

```
In [94]: dfa.select("A", C=pd.col("A") + pd.col("B"), D=pd.col("C") * 2)
Out[94]: 
   A  C   D
0  1  5  10
1  2  7  14
2  3  9  18
```
See [Selecting columns with select](https://pandas.pydata.org/indexing.html#indexing-select) for more.

payload.content:
## Indexing / selection[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-selection)

The basics of indexing are as follows:

| Operation | Syntax | Result | 
|---|---|---|
| Select column | `df[col]` | Series | 
| Select row by label | `df.loc[label]` | Series | 
| Select row by integer location | `df.iloc[loc]` | Series | 
| Slice rows | `df[5:10]` | DataFrame | 
| Select rows by boolean vector | `df[bool_vec]` | DataFrame | 

Row selection, for example, returns a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) whose index is the columns of the
[`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame):

```
In [95]: df.loc["b"]
Out[95]: 
one            2.0
bar            2.0
flag         False
foo            bar
one_trunc      2.0
Name: b, dtype: object
In [96]: df.iloc[2]
Out[96]: 
one           3.0
bar           3.0
flag         True
foo           bar
one_trunc     NaN
Name: c, dtype: object
```
For a more exhaustive treatment of sophisticated label-based indexing and
slicing, see the [section on indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/indexing.html#indexing). We will address the
fundamentals of reindexing / conforming to new sets of labels in the
[section on reindexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics-reindexing).

## Data alignment and arithmetic[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#data-alignment-and-arithmetic)

Data alignment between [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) objects automatically align on **both the
columns and the index (row labels)**. Again, the resulting object will have the
union of the column and row labels.

```
In [97]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(10, 4), columns=["A", "B", "C", "D"])
In [98]: df2 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(7, 3), columns=["A", "B", "C"])
In [99]: df + df2
Out[99]: 
          A         B         C   D
0  0.045691 -0.014138  1.380871 NaN
1 -0.955398 -1.501007  0.037181 NaN
2 -0.662690  1.534833 -0.859691 NaN
3 -2.452949  1.237274 -0.133712 NaN
4  1.414490  1.951676 -2.320422 NaN
5 -0.494922 -1.649727 -1.084601 NaN
6 -1.047551 -0.748572 -0.805479 NaN
7       NaN       NaN       NaN NaN
8       NaN       NaN       NaN NaN
9       NaN       NaN       NaN NaN
```
When doing an operation between [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) and [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series), the default behavior is
to align the `Series`**index** on the `DataFrame`**columns**, thus [broadcasting](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.broadcasting.html)
row-wise. For example:

```
In [100]: df - df.iloc[0]
Out[100]:

0  0.000000  0.000000  0.000000  0.000000

indexing semantics and data model are quite different in places from an n-dimensional
array.

payload.content:
indexing semantics and data model are quite different in places from an n-dimensional
array.

[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) implements `__array_ufunc__`, which allows it to work with NumPy’s
[universal functions](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/ufuncs.html).

The ufunc is applied to the underlying array in a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series).

```
In [113]: ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
In [114]: np.exp(ser)
Out[114]: 
0     2.718282
1     7.389056
2    20.085537
3    54.598150
dtype: float64
```
When multiple [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) are passed to a ufunc, they are aligned before
performing the operation.

Like other parts of the library, pandas will automatically align labeled inputs
as part of a ufunc with multiple inputs. For example, using `numpy.remainder()`
on two [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) with differently ordered labels will align before the operation.

```
In [115]: ser1 = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=["a", "b", "c"])
In [116]: ser2 = pd.Series([1, 3, 5], index=["b", "a", "c"])
In [117]: ser1
Out[117]: 
a    1
b    2
c    3
dtype: int64
In [118]: ser2
Out[118]: 
b    1
a    3
c    5
dtype: int64
In [119]: np.remainder(ser1, ser2)
Out[119]: 
a    1
b    0
c    3
dtype: int64
```
As usual, the union of the two indices is taken, and non-overlapping values are filled with missing values.

```
In [120]: ser3 = pd.Series([2, 4, 6], index=["b", "c", "d"])
In [121]: ser3
Out[121]: 
b    2
c    4
d    6
dtype: int64
In [122]: np.remainder(ser1, ser3)
Out[122]: 
a    NaN
b    0.0
c    3.0
d    NaN
dtype: float64
```

Out[121]: 
b    2

a    NaN

When a binary ufunc is applied to a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) and [`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index), the [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series)
implementation takes precedence and a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) is returned.

```
In [123]: ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
In [124]: idx = pd.Index([4, 5, 6])
In [125]: np.maximum(ser, idx)
Out[125]: 
0    4
1    5
2    6
dtype: int64
```
NumPy ufuncs are safe to apply to [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) backed by non-ndarray arrays,
for example [`arrays.SparseArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.arrays.SparseArray.html#pandas.arrays.SparseArray) (see [Sparse calculation](https://pandas.pydata.org/sparse.html#sparse-calculation)). If possible,
the ufunc is applied without converting the underlying data to an ndarray.

A very large [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) will be truncated to display them in the console.

(The **baseball** dataset is from the **plyr** R package):

```

In [127]: print(baseball)

payload.content:
## Indexing and selecting data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-and-selecting-data)

The axis labeling information in pandas objects serves many purposes:

- Identifies data (i.e. provides *metadata*) using known indicators,
important for analysis, visualization, and interactive console display.
- Enables automatic and explicit data alignment.
- Allows intuitive getting and setting of subsets of the data set.

In this section, we will focus on the final point: namely, how to slice, dice, and generally get and set subsets of pandas objects. The primary focus will be on Series and DataFrame as they have received more development attention in this area.

Note

The Python and NumPy indexing operators `[]` and attribute operator `.`
provide quick and easy access to pandas data structures across a wide range
of use cases. This makes interactive work intuitive, as there’s little new
to learn if you already know how to deal with Python dictionaries and NumPy
arrays. However, since the type of the data to be accessed isn’t known in
advance, directly using standard operators has some optimization limits. For
production code, we recommended that you take advantage of the optimized
pandas data access methods exposed in this chapter.

See the [MultiIndex / Advanced Indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced) for `MultiIndex` and more advanced indexing documentation.

See the [cookbook](https://pandas.pydata.org/cookbook.html#cookbook-selection) for some advanced strategies.

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Indexing and selecting data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-and-selecting-data) > Different choices for indexing[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#different-choices-for-indexing)
payload.content:
## Different choices for indexing[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#different-choices-for-indexing)

Object selection has had a number of user-requested additions in order to support more explicit location based indexing. pandas now supports three types of multi-axis indexing.

- `.loc` is primarily label based, but may also be used with a boolean array. `.loc` will raise `KeyError` when the items are not found. Allowed inputs are:
  - A single label, e.g. `5` or `'a'` (Note that `5` is interpreted as a *label* of the index. This use is **not** an integer position along the
index.).
  - A list or array of labels `['a', 'b', 'c']`.
  - A slice object with labels `'a':'f'` (Note that contrary to usual Python
slices, **both** the start and the stop are included, when present in the
index! See [Slicing with labels](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-slicing-with-labels) and [Endpoints are inclusive](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced-endpoints-are-inclusive).)
  - A boolean array (any `NA` values will be treated as `False`).
  - A `callable` function with one argument (the calling Series or DataFrame) and
that returns valid output for indexing (one of the above).
  - A tuple of row (and column) indices whose elements are one of the above inputs.
See more at [Selection by Label](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-label).
- `.iloc` is primarily integer position based (from `0` to `length-1` of the axis), but may also be used with a boolean
array. `.iloc` will raise `IndexError` if a requested
indexer is out-of-bounds, except *slice* indexers which allow
out-of-bounds indexing.  (this conforms with Python/NumPy *slice* semantics).  Allowed inputs are:
  - An integer e.g. `5`.
  - A list or array of integers `[4, 3, 0]`.
  - A slice object with ints `1:7`.

payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Indexing and selecting data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-and-selecting-data) > Different choices for indexing[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#different-choices-for-indexing)
payload.content:
out-of-bounds indexing.  (this conforms with Python/NumPy *slice* semantics).  Allowed inputs are:
  - An integer e.g. `5`.
  - A list or array of integers `[4, 3, 0]`.
  - A slice object with ints `1:7`.
  - A boolean array (any `NA` values will be treated as `False`).
  - A `callable` function with one argument (the calling Series or DataFrame) and
that returns valid output for indexing (one of the above).
  - A tuple of row (and column) indices whose elements are one of the above inputs.
See more at [Selection by Position](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-integer), [Advanced Indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced) and [Advanced
Hierarchical](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced-advanced-hierarchical).
- `.loc`, `.iloc`, and also `[]` indexing can accept a `callable` as indexer. See more at [Selection By Callable](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-callable).
Note Destructuring tuple keys into row (and column) indexes occurs
*before* callables are applied, so you cannot return a tuple from
a callable to index both rows and columns.

Getting values from an object with multi-axes selection uses the following
notation (using `.loc` as an example, but the following applies to `.iloc` as
well). Any of the axes accessors may be the null slice `:`. Axes left out of
the specification are assumed to be `:`, e.g. `p.loc['a']` is equivalent to
`p.loc['a', :]`.

```
In [1]: ser = pd.Series(range(5), index=list("abcde"))
In [2]: ser.loc[["a", "c", "e"]]
Out[2]: 
a    0
c    2
e    4
dtype: int64
In [3]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(25).reshape(5, 5), index=list("abcde"), columns=list("abcde"))
In [4]: df.loc[["a", "c", "e"], ["b", "d"]]
Out[4]: 
    b   d
a   1   3
c  11  13
e  21  23
```

payload.content:
## Basics[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#basics)

As mentioned when introducing the data structures in the [last section](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics), the primary function of indexing with `[]` (a.k.a. `__getitem__`
for those familiar with implementing class behavior in Python) is selecting out
lower-dimensional slices. The following table shows return type values when
indexing pandas objects with `[]`:

| Object Type | Selection | Return Value Type | 
|---|---|---|
| Series | `series[label]` | scalar value | 
| DataFrame | `frame[colname]` | `Series` corresponding to colname | 
| DataFrame | `frame[[colname]]` | `DataFrame` with columns corresponding to `[colname]` | 
| DataFrame | `frame[list_of_colnames]` | `DataFrame` with columns corresponding to `list_of_colnames` | 

The same principle applies to label-based selection with `.loc`: a
list-like of labels preserves the corresponding axis (so
`df.loc[:, ["A"]]` returns a `DataFrame`, even when the list contains a
single label), while a scalar label reduces the axis when labels on that
axis are unique (so `df.loc[:, "A"]` typically returns a `Series`; if
`"A"` is duplicated on the axis, a `DataFrame` is returned instead).
See [Selection by label](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-label) for details.

Here we construct a simple time series data set to use for illustrating the indexing functionality:

```
In [5]: dates = pd.date_range('1/1/2000', periods=8)
In [6]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 4),
   ...:                   index=dates, columns=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'])
   ...: 
In [7]: df
Out[7]: 
                   A         B         C         D
2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863 -1.509059 -1.135632
2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  1.071804

payload.content:
## Selecting columns with `select`[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selecting-columns-with-select)

[`DataFrame.select()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.select.html#pandas.DataFrame.select) returns a DataFrame with the requested columns in the
given order, similar to passing a list of columns to `[]`. As a method, it
can be used within a chain of operations. Columns can be given as individual
arguments or as a single list:

```
In [21]: df.select('B', 'A')
Out[21]: 
                   B         A
2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863
2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648
2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046
2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892
In [22]: df.select(['B', 'A'])
Out[22]: 
                   B         A
2000-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863
2000-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
2000-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
2000-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
2000-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648
2000-01-07  0.404705  0.577046
2000-01-08 -0.370647 -1.157892
```
In addition to existing columns, computed columns can be included via
[`pandas.col()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.col.html#pandas.col) expressions or callables. A positional expression keeps the
name of the underlying column, while a keyword argument names the resulting
column. Later arguments can refer to columns computed earlier in the same call:

```
In [23]: df.select('A', pd.col('B') * 2, C=pd.col('A') + pd.col('B'), D=pd.col('C') > 0)
Out[23]: 
                   A         B         C      D
2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.938225  0.655361   True
2000-01-02 -0.173215  2.424224  2.251009   True
2000-01-03 -2.104569 -1.723698 -3.828267  False

2000-01-07  6  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268

```
Warning

- You can use this access only if the index element is a valid Python identifier, e.g. `s.1` is not allowed.
See [here for an explanation of valid identifiers](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#identifiers).
- The attribute will not be available if it conflicts with an existing method name, e.g. `s.min` is not allowed, but `s['min']` is possible.
- Similarly, the attribute will not be available if it conflicts with any of the following list: `index`, `major_axis`, `minor_axis`, `items`.
- In any of these cases, standard indexing will still work, e.g. `s['1']`, `s['min']`, and `s['index']` will
access the corresponding element or column.

If you are using the IPython environment, you may also use tab-completion to see these accessible attributes.

You can also assign a `dict` to a row of a `DataFrame`:

```
In [35]: x = pd.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2, 3], 'y': [3, 4, 5]})
In [36]: x.iloc[1] = {'x': 9, 'y': 99}
In [37]: x
Out[37]: 
   x   y
0  1   3
1  9  99
2  3   5
```
You can use attribute access to modify an existing element of a Series or column of a DataFrame, but be careful;
if you try to use attribute access to create a new column, it creates a new attribute rather than a
new column and will this raise a `UserWarning`:

```
In [38]: df_new = pd.DataFrame({'one': [1., 2., 3.]})
In [39]: df_new.two = [4, 5, 6]
In [40]: df_new
Out[40]: 
   one
0  1.0
1  2.0
2  3.0
```

payload.content:
## Slicing ranges[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#slicing-ranges)

The most robust and consistent way of slicing ranges along arbitrary axes is
described in the [Selection by Position](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-integer) section
detailing the `.iloc` method. For now, we explain the semantics of slicing using the `[]` operator.

With Series, the syntax works exactly as with an ndarray, returning a slice of the values and the corresponding labels:

```
In [41]: s[:5]
Out[41]: 
2000-01-01    0.469112
2000-01-02    1.212112
2000-01-03   -0.861849
2000-01-04    0.721555
2000-01-05   -0.424972
Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64
In [42]: s[::2]
Out[42]: 
2000-01-01    0.469112
2000-01-03   -0.861849
2000-01-05   -0.424972
2000-01-07    0.404705
Freq: 2D, Name: A, dtype: float64
In [43]: s[::-1]
Out[43]: 
2000-01-08   -0.370647
2000-01-07    0.404705
2000-01-06   -0.673690
2000-01-05   -0.424972
2000-01-04    0.721555
2000-01-03   -0.861849
2000-01-02    1.212112
2000-01-01    0.469112
Freq: -1D, Name: A, dtype: float64
```
Note that setting works as well:

```
In [44]: s2 = s.copy()
In [45]: s2[:5] = 0
In [46]: s2
Out[46]: 
2000-01-01    0.000000
2000-01-02    0.000000
2000-01-03    0.000000
2000-01-04    0.000000
2000-01-05    0.000000
2000-01-06   -0.673690
2000-01-07    0.404705
2000-01-08   -0.370647
Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64
```
With DataFrame, slicing inside of `[]` **slices the rows**. This is provided
largely as a convenience since it is such a common operation.

```
In [47]: df[:3]
Out[47]: 
                   A         B         C         D
2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112 -1.509059 -1.135632
2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112  0.119209 -1.044236
2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849 -0.494929  1.071804
In [48]: df[::-1]
Out[48]:

## Selection by label[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selection-by-label)

Warning

`.loc` is strict when you present slicers that are not compatible (or convertible) with the index type. For example
using integers in a `DatetimeIndex`. These will raise a `TypeError`.

payload.content:
String likes in slicing *can* be convertible to the type of the index and lead to natural slicing.

```
In [52]: dfl.loc['20130102':'20130104']
Out[52]: 
                   A         B         C         D
2013-01-02  0.357021 -0.674600 -1.776904 -0.968914
2013-01-03 -1.294524  0.413738  0.276662 -0.472035
2013-01-04 -0.013960 -0.362543 -0.006154 -0.923061
```
pandas provides a suite of methods in order to have **purely label based indexing**. This is a strict inclusion based protocol.
Every label asked for must be in the index, or a `KeyError` will be raised.
When slicing, both the start bound **AND** the stop bound are *included*, if present in the index.
Integers are valid labels, but they refer to the label **and not the position**.

The `.loc` attribute is the primary access method. The following are valid inputs:

- A single label, e.g. `5` or `'a'` (Note that `5` is interpreted as a *label* of the index. This use is **not** an integer position along the index.).
- A list or array of labels `['a', 'b', 'c']`.
- A slice object with labels `'a':'f'`. Note that contrary to usual Python
slices, **both** the start and the stop are included, when present in the
index! See [Slicing with labels](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-slicing-with-labels).
- A boolean array.
- A `callable`, see [Selection By Callable](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-callable).

```
In [53]: s1 = pd.Series(np.random.randn(6), index=list('abcdef'))
In [54]: s1
Out[54]: 
a    1.431256
b    1.340309
c   -1.170299
d   -0.226169
e    0.410835
f    0.813850
dtype: float64
In [55]: s1.loc['c':]
Out[55]: 
c   -1.170299
d   -0.226169
e    0.410835
f    0.813850
dtype: float64
In [56]: s1.loc['b']
Out[56]: np.float64(1.3403088497993827)
```

payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > this is also equivalent to ``df1.at['a','A']`` > Slicing with labels[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#slicing-with-labels)
payload.content:
## Slicing with labels[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#slicing-with-labels)

When using `.loc` with slices, if both the start and the stop labels are
present in the index, then elements *located* between the two (including them)
are returned:

```
In [70]: s = pd.Series(list('abcde'), index=[0, 3, 2, 5, 4])
In [71]: s.loc[3:5]
Out[71]: 
3    b
2    c
5    d
dtype: str
```
If the index is sorted, and can be compared against start and stop labels,
then slicing will still work as expected, by selecting labels which *rank*
between the two:

```
In [72]: s.sort_index()
Out[72]: 
0    a
2    c
3    b
4    e
5    d
dtype: str
In [73]: s.sort_index().loc[1:6]
Out[73]: 
2    c
3    b
4    e
5    d
dtype: str
```
However, if at least one of the two is absent *and* the index is not sorted, an
error will be raised (since doing otherwise would be computationally expensive,
as well as potentially ambiguous for mixed type indexes). For instance, in the
above example, `s.loc[1:6]` would raise `KeyError`.

For the rationale behind this behavior, see
[Endpoints are inclusive](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced-endpoints-are-inclusive).

```
In [74]: s = pd.Series(list('abcdef'), index=[0, 3, 2, 5, 4, 2])
In [75]: s.loc[3:5]
Out[75]: 
3    b
2    c
5    d
dtype: str
```
Also, if the index has duplicate labels *and* either the start or the stop label is duplicated,
an error will be raised. For instance, in the above example, `s.loc[2:5]` would raise a `KeyError`.

For more information about duplicate labels, see
[Duplicate Labels](https://pandas.pydata.org/duplicates.html#duplicates).

When using a slice with a step, such as `.loc[start:stop:step]`, note that
*start* and *stop* are interpreted as **labels**, while *step* is applied over

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > this is also equivalent to ``df1.at['a','A']`` > Slicing with labels[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#slicing-with-labels)
payload.content:
[Duplicate Labels](https://pandas.pydata.org/duplicates.html#duplicates).

When using a slice with a step, such as `.loc[start:stop:step]`, note that
*start* and *stop* are interpreted as **labels**, while *step* is applied over
the **positional index** within that label range. This means a stepped slice
will behave differently than using the labels `range(start, stop, step)` when
the index is not contiguous integers.

For example, in a `Series` with a non-contiguous integer index:

```
In [76]: s = pd.Series(range(10), index=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45])
In [77]: s.loc[10:50:5]              # (10), then skip 5 positions → 35 only
Out[77]: 
10    2
35    7
dtype: int64
In [78]: s.loc[[10, 15, 20, 25]]     # explicit label selection
Out[78]: 
10    2
15    3
20    4
25    5
dtype: int64
```
The first applies *step* across **positional locations** between the start/stop
labels. The second selects each label directly.

Similarly, with a string-based index, the behavior is identical:

```
In [79]: s = pd.Series(range(10), index=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g', 'h', 'i', 'j'])
In [80]: s.loc['b':'i':2]            # Start at 'b' (position 1), stop at 'i' (position 8), step 2 positions → 'b', 'd', 'f', 'h'
Out[80]: 
b    1
d    3
f    5
h    7
dtype: int64
In [81]: s.loc[['b', 'd', 'f', 'h']] # explicit label selection
Out[81]: 
b    1
d    3
f    5
h    7
dtype: int64
```
In both cases, *start* and *stop* determine the label boundaries (inclusive),
while *step* skips positions within that range, regardless of the index type.

payload.content:
## Selection by position[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selection-by-position)

pandas provides a suite of methods in order to get **purely integer based indexing**. The semantics follow closely Python and NumPy slicing. These are `0-based` indexing. When slicing, the start bound is *included*, while the upper bound is *excluded*. Trying to use a non-integer, even a **valid** label will raise an `IndexError`.

The `.iloc` attribute is the primary access method. The following are valid inputs:

- An integer e.g. `5`.
- A list or array of integers `[4, 3, 0]`.
- A slice object with ints `1:7`.
- A boolean array.
- A `callable`, see [Selection By Callable](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-callable).
- A tuple of row (and column) indexes, whose elements are one of the above types.

```
In [82]: s1 = pd.Series(np.random.randn(5), index=list(range(0, 10, 2)))
In [83]: s1
Out[83]: 
0    0.695775
2    0.341734
4    0.959726
6   -1.110336
8   -0.619976
dtype: float64
In [84]: s1.iloc[:3]
Out[84]: 
0    0.695775
2    0.341734
4    0.959726
dtype: float64
In [85]: s1.iloc[3]
Out[85]: np.float64(-1.110336102891167)
```
Note that setting works as well:

```
In [86]: s1.iloc[:3] = 0
In [87]: s1
Out[87]: 
0    0.000000
2    0.000000
4    0.000000
6   -1.110336
8   -0.619976
dtype: float64
```
With a DataFrame:

```
In [88]: df1 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(6, 4),
   ....:                    index=list(range(0, 12, 2)),
   ....:                    columns=list(range(0, 8, 2)))
   ....: 
In [89]: df1
Out[89]: 
           0         2         4         6
0   0.149748 -0.732339  0.687738  0.176444
2   0.403310 -0.154951  0.301624 -2.179861
4  -1.369849 -0.954208  1.462696 -1.743161
6  -0.826591 -0.345352  1.314232  0.690579

payload.content:
## Selection by callable[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selection-by-callable)

`.loc`, `.iloc`, and also `[]` indexing can accept a `callable` as indexer.
The `callable` must be a function with one argument (the calling Series or DataFrame) that returns valid output for indexing.

Note

For `.iloc` indexing, returning a tuple from the callable is
not supported, since tuple destructuring for row and column indexes
occurs *before* applying callables.

```
In [112]: df1 = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(6, 4),
   .....:                    index=list('abcdef'),
   .....:                    columns=list('ABCD'))
   .....: 
In [113]: df1
Out[113]: 
          A         B         C         D
a -0.023688  2.410179  1.450520  0.206053
b -0.251905 -2.213588  1.063327  1.266143
c  0.299368 -0.863838  0.408204 -1.048089
d -0.025747 -0.988387  0.094055  1.262731
e  1.289997  0.082423 -0.055758  0.536580
f -0.489682  0.369374 -0.034571 -2.484478
In [114]: df1.loc[lambda df: df['A'] > 0, :]
Out[114]: 
          A         B         C         D
c  0.299368 -0.863838  0.408204 -1.048089
e  1.289997  0.082423 -0.055758  0.536580
In [115]: df1.loc[:, lambda df: ['A', 'B']]
Out[115]: 
          A         B
a -0.023688  2.410179
b -0.251905 -2.213588
c  0.299368 -0.863838
d -0.025747 -0.988387
e  1.289997  0.082423
f -0.489682  0.369374
In [116]: df1.iloc[:, lambda df: [0, 1]]
Out[116]: 
          A         B
a -0.023688  2.410179
b -0.251905 -2.213588
c  0.299368 -0.863838
d -0.025747 -0.988387
e  1.289997  0.082423
f -0.489682  0.369374
In [117]: df1[lambda df: df.columns[0]]
Out[117]: 
a   -0.023688
b   -0.251905
c    0.299368
d   -0.025747
e    1.289997
f   -0.489682
Name: A, dtype: float64
```
You can use callable indexing in `Series`.

```
In [118]: df1['A'].loc[lambda s: s > 0]
Out[118]:

payload.content:
## Combining positional and label-based indexing[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#combining-positional-and-label-based-indexing)

If you wish to get the 0th and the 2nd elements from the index in the ‘A’ column, you can do:

```
In [121]: dfd = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3],
   .....:                     'B': [4, 5, 6]},
   .....:                    index=list('abc'))
   .....: 
In [122]: dfd
Out[122]: 
   A  B
a  1  4
b  2  5
c  3  6
In [123]: dfd.loc[dfd.index[[0, 2]], 'A']
Out[123]: 
a    1
c    3
Name: A, dtype: int64
```
This can also be expressed using `.iloc`, by explicitly getting locations on the indexers, and using
*positional* indexing to select things.

```
In [124]: dfd.iloc[[0, 2], dfd.columns.get_loc('A')]
Out[124]: 
a    1
c    3
Name: A, dtype: int64
```
For getting *multiple* indexers, using `.get_indexer`:

```
In [125]: dfd.iloc[[0, 2], dfd.columns.get_indexer(['A', 'B'])]
Out[125]: 
   A  B
a  1  4
c  3  6
```

payload.content:
## Reindexing[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#reindexing)

The idiomatic way to achieve selecting potentially not-found elements is via `.reindex()`. See also the section on [reindexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics-reindexing).

```
In [126]: s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
In [127]: s.reindex([1, 2, 3])
Out[127]: 
1    2.0
2    3.0
3    NaN
dtype: float64
```
Alternatively, if you want to select only *valid* keys, the following is idiomatic and efficient; it is guaranteed to preserve the dtype of the selection.

```
In [128]: labels = [1, 2, 3]
In [129]: s.loc[s.index.intersection(labels)]
Out[129]: 
1    2
2    3
dtype: int64
```
Having a duplicated index will raise for a `.reindex()`:

```
In [130]: s = pd.Series(np.arange(4), index=['a', 'a', 'b', 'c'])
In [131]: labels = ['c', 'd']

payload.content:
## Selecting random samples[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selecting-random-samples)

A random selection of rows or columns from a Series or DataFrame with the [`sample()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sample.html#pandas.DataFrame.sample) method. The method will sample rows by default, and accepts a specific number of rows/columns to return, or a fraction of rows.

```
In [136]: s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.section: When no arguments are passed, returns 1 row.
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > When no arguments are passed, returns 1 row.
payload.content:
## When no arguments are passed, returns 1 row.

In [137]: s.sample()
Out[137]: 
4    4
dtype: int64

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.section: One may specify either a number of rows:
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > One may specify either a number of rows:
payload.content:
## One may specify either a number of rows:

In [138]: s.sample(n=3)
Out[138]: 
0    0
4    4
1    1
dtype: int64

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.section: Or a fraction of the rows:
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Or a fraction of the rows:
payload.content:
## Or a fraction of the rows:

In [139]: s.sample(frac=0.5)
Out[139]: 
5    5
3    3
1    1
dtype: int64
```
By default, `sample` will return each row at most once, but one can also sample with replacement
using the `replace` option:

```
In [140]: s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Without replacement (default):
payload.content:
## Without replacement (default):

In [141]: s.sample(n=6, replace=False)
Out[141]: 
0    0
1    1
5    5
3    3
2    2
4    4
dtype: int64

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > With replacement:
payload.content:
## With replacement:

In [142]: s.sample(n=6, replace=True)
Out[142]: 
0    0
4    4
3    3
2    2
4    4
4    4
dtype: int64
```
By default, each row has an equal probability of being selected, but if you want rows
to have different probabilities, you can pass the `sample` function sampling weights as
`weights`. These weights can be a list, a NumPy array, or a Series, but they must be of the same length as the object you are sampling. Missing values will be treated as a weight of zero, and inf values are not allowed. If weights do not sum to 1, they will be re-normalized by dividing all weights by the sum of the weights. For example:

```
In [143]: s = pd.Series([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
In [144]: example_weights = [0, 0, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.4]
In [145]: s.sample(n=2, weights=example_weights)
Out[145]: 
5    5
4    4
dtype: int64

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Weights will be re-normalized automatically
payload.content:
## Weights will be re-normalized automatically

In [146]: example_weights2 = [0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
In [147]: s.sample(n=1, weights=example_weights2)
Out[147]: 
0    0
dtype: int64
```
When applied to a DataFrame, you can use a column of the DataFrame as sampling weights (provided you are sampling rows and not columns) by simply passing the name of the column as a string.

```
In [148]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({'col1': [9, 8, 7, 6],
   .....:                     'weight_column': [0.5, 0.4, 0.1, 0]})
   .....: 
In [149]: df2.sample(n=2, weights='weight_column')
Out[149]: 
   col1  weight_column
0     9            0.5
1     8            0.4
```
`sample` also allows users to sample columns instead of rows using the `axis` argument.

```
In [150]: df3 = pd.DataFrame({'col1': [1, 2, 3], 'col2': [2, 3, 4]})
In [151]: df3.sample(n=1, axis=1)
Out[151]: 
   col2
0     2
1     3
2     4
```
Finally, one can also set a seed for `sample`’s random number generator using the `random_state` argument, which will accept either an integer (as a seed) or a NumPy RandomState object.

```
In [152]: df4 = pd.DataFrame({'col1': [1, 2, 3], 'col2': [2, 3, 4]})

payload.content:
## With a given seed, the sample will always draw the same rows.

In [153]: df4.sample(n=2, random_state=2)
Out[153]: 
   col1  col2
2     3     4
1     2     3
In [154]: df4.sample(n=2, random_state=2)
Out[154]: 
   col1  col2
2     3     4
1     2     3
```

payload.content:
## Setting with enlargement[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#setting-with-enlargement)

The `.loc/[]` operations can perform enlargement when setting a non-existent key for that axis.

In the `Series` case this is effectively an appending operation.

```
In [155]: se = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
In [156]: se
Out[156]: 
0    1
1    2
2    3
dtype: int64
In [157]: se[5] = 5.
In [158]: se
Out[158]: 
0    1
1    2
2    3
5    5
dtype: int64
```
A `DataFrame` can be enlarged on either axis via `.loc`.

```
In [159]: dfi = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2),
   .....:                    columns=['A', 'B'])
   .....: 
In [160]: dfi
Out[160]: 
   A  B
0  0  1
1  2  3
2  4  5
In [161]: dfi.loc[:, 'C'] = dfi.loc[:, 'A']
In [162]: dfi
Out[162]: 
   A  B  C
0  0  1  0
1  2  3  2
2  4  5  4
```
This is like an `append` operation on the `DataFrame`.

```
In [163]: dfi.loc[3] = 5
In [164]: dfi
Out[164]: 
   A  B  C
0  0  1  0
1  2  3  2
2  4  5  4
3  5  5  5
```

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > With a given seed, the sample will always draw the same rows. > Fast scalar value getting and setting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#fast-scalar-value-getting-and-setting)
payload.content:
## Fast scalar value getting and setting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#fast-scalar-value-getting-and-setting)

Since indexing with `[]` must handle a lot of cases (single-label access,
slicing, boolean indexing, etc.), it has a bit of overhead in order to figure
out what you’re asking for. If you only want to access a scalar value, the
fastest way is to use the `at` and `iat` methods, which are implemented on
all of the data structures.

Similarly to `loc`, `at` provides **label** based scalar lookups, while, `iat` provides **integer** based lookups analogously to `iloc`

```
In [165]: s.iat[5]
Out[165]: np.int64(5)
In [166]: df.at[dates[5], 'A']
Out[166]: np.float64(0.1136484096888855)
In [167]: df.iat[3, 0]
Out[167]: np.float64(-0.7067711336300845)
```
You can also set using these same indexers.

```
In [168]: df.at[dates[5], 'A'] = 7
In [169]: df.iat[3, 0] = 7
```
`at` previously could enlarge the object in-place if the indexer was missing,
but this behavior is deprecated. Use `.loc` instead for setting values with
new keys:

```
In [170]: df.loc[dates[-1] + pd.Timedelta('1 day'), 0] = 7
In [171]: df
Out[171]: 
                   A         B         C         D    0
2000-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112 -1.509059 -1.135632  NaN
2000-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112  0.119209 -1.044236  NaN
2000-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849 -0.494929  1.071804  NaN
2000-01-04  7.000000  0.721555 -1.039575  0.271860  NaN
2000-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972  0.276232 -1.087401  NaN
2000-01-06  7.000000 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988  NaN
2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268  NaN
2000-01-08 -1.157892 -0.370647 -1.344312  0.844885  NaN
2000-01-09       NaN       NaN       NaN       NaN  7.0
```

payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > With a given seed, the sample will always draw the same rows. > Boolean indexing[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#boolean-indexing)
payload.content:
## Boolean indexing[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#boolean-indexing)

Another common operation is the use of boolean vectors to filter the data.
The operators are: `|` for `or`, `&` for `and`, and `~` for `not`.
These **must** be grouped by using parentheses, since by default Python will
evaluate an expression such as `df['A'] > 2 & df['B'] < 3` as
`df['A'] > (2 & df['B']) < 3`, while the desired evaluation order is
`(df['A'] > 2) & (df['B'] < 3)`.

Using a boolean vector to index a Series works exactly as in a NumPy ndarray:

```
In [172]: s = pd.Series(range(-3, 4))
In [173]: s
Out[173]: 
0   -3
1   -2
2   -1
3    0
4    1
5    2
6    3
dtype: int64
In [174]: s[s > 0]
Out[174]: 
4    1
5    2
6    3
dtype: int64
In [175]: s[(s < -1) | (s > 0.5)]
Out[175]: 
0   -3
1   -2
4    1
5    2
6    3
dtype: int64
In [176]: s[~(s < 0)]
Out[176]: 
3    0
4    1
5    2
6    3
dtype: int64

```
In [177]: df[df['A'] > 0]

2000-01-04  7.000000  0.721555 -1.039575  0.271860 NaN

2000-01-06  7.000000 -0.673690 -1.478427  0.524988 NaN
2000-01-07  0.577046  0.404705 -1.715002 -1.039268 NaN
```

more complex criteria:

```
In [178]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({'a': ['one', 'one', 'two', 'three', 'two', 'one', 'six'],
   .....:                     'b': ['x', 'y', 'y', 'x', 'y', 'x', 'x'],

payload.content:
## Filtering with `DataFrame.filter`[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#filtering-with-dataframe-filter)

Added in version 3.1.0.

[`DataFrame.filter()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.filter.html#pandas.DataFrame.filter) and [`Series.filter()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.filter.html#pandas.Series.filter) also accept a boolean mask
through the `cond` keyword, keeping the rows where the mask is True. A
[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) mask is aligned on the index; any other array-like must have
the same length as the index.

```
In [189]: df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3], 'B': [4, 5, 6]}, index=list('abc'))
In [190]: df.filter(cond=df['A'] > 1)
Out[190]: 
   A  B
b  2  5
c  3  6
```
`cond` may also be a callable that returns a boolean mask, or an expression
created with [`pandas.col()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.col.html#pandas.col). These two forms may be passed positionally,
which is convenient in a method chain where the intermediate object has no
name:

```
In [191]: df.filter(pd.col('A') > 1)
Out[191]: 
   A  B
b  2  5
c  3  6
In [192]: df.assign(C=pd.col('A') + pd.col('B')).filter(lambda df: df['C'] > 5)
Out[192]: 
   A  B  C
b  2  5  7
c  3  6  9
```
Pass `axis=1` to filter columns instead of rows:

```
In [193]: df.filter(cond=df.columns.str.startswith('A'), axis=1)
Out[193]: 
   A
a  1
b  2
c  3
```
Missing values in the mask are treated as False by default, matching
`df[mask]` for a mask with nullable boolean dtype. Pass `na=True` to keep
the corresponding rows instead, or `na="raise"` to raise an error:

```
In [194]: mask = pd.array([True, None, False], dtype="boolean")
In [195]: df.filter(cond=mask)
Out[195]: 
   A  B
a  1  4

payload.content:
## Indexing with isin[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#indexing-with-isin)

Consider the [`isin()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.isin.html#pandas.Series.isin) method of `Series`, which returns a boolean
vector that is true wherever the `Series` elements exist in the passed list.
This allows you to select rows where one or more columns have values you want:

```
In [197]: s = pd.Series(np.arange(5), index=np.arange(5)[::-1], dtype='int64')
In [198]: s
Out[198]: 
4    0
3    1
2    2
1    3
0    4
dtype: int64
In [199]: s.isin([2, 4, 6])
Out[199]: 
4    False
3    False
2     True
1    False
0     True
dtype: bool
In [200]: s[s.isin([2, 4, 6])]
Out[200]: 
2    2
0    4
dtype: int64
```
The same method is available for `Index` objects and is useful for the cases
when you don’t know which of the sought labels are in fact present:

```
In [201]: s[s.index.isin([2, 4, 6])]
Out[201]: 
4    0
2    2
dtype: int64
