## compare it to the following

In [202]: s.reindex([2, 4, 6])
Out[202]: 
2    2.0
4    0.0
6    NaN
dtype: float64
```
In addition to that, `MultiIndex` allows selecting a separate level to use
in the membership check:

```
In [203]: s_mi = pd.Series(np.arange(6),
   .....:                  index=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([[0, 1], ['a', 'b', 'c']]))
   .....: 
In [204]: s_mi
Out[204]: 
0  a    0
   b    1
   c    2
1  a    3
   b    4
   c    5
dtype: int64
In [205]: s_mi.iloc[s_mi.index.isin([(1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (0, 'c')])]
Out[205]: 
0  c    2
1  a    3
dtype: int64
In [206]: s_mi.iloc[s_mi.index.isin(['a', 'c', 'e'], level=1)]
Out[206]: 
0  a    0
   c    2
1  a    3
   c    5
dtype: int64
```
DataFrame also has an [`isin()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.isin.html#pandas.DataFrame.isin) method.  When calling `isin`, pass a set of
values as either an array or dict.  If values is an array, `isin` returns
a DataFrame of booleans that is the same shape as the original DataFrame, with True
wherever the element is in the sequence of values.

```
In [207]: df = pd.DataFrame({'vals': [1, 2, 3, 4], 'ids': ['a', 'b', 'f', 'n'],
   .....:                    'ids2': ['a', 'n', 'c', 'n']})
   .....: 
In [208]: values = ['a', 'b', 1, 3]
In [209]: df.isin(values)
Out[209]: 
    vals    ids   ids2
0   True   True   True
1  False   True  False
2   True  False  False
3  False  False  False
```
Oftentimes you’ll want to match certain values with certain columns.
Just make values a `dict` where the key is the column, and the value is
a list of items you want to check for.

```
In [210]: values = {'ids': ['a', 'b'], 'vals': [1, 3]}
In [211]: df.isin(values)
Out[211]: 
    vals    ids   ids2
0   True   True  False
1  False   True  False

```
In [210]: values = {'ids': ['a', 'b'], 'vals': [1, 3]}
In [211]: df.isin(values)
Out[211]: 
    vals    ids   ids2
0   True   True  False
1  False   True  False
2   True  False  False
3  False  False  False
```
To return the DataFrame of booleans where the values are *not* in the original DataFrame,
use the `~` operator:

```
In [212]: values = {'ids': ['a', 'b'], 'vals': [1, 3]}
In [213]: ~df.isin(values)
Out[213]: 
    vals    ids  ids2
0  False  False  True
1   True  False  True
2  False   True  True
3   True   True  True
```
Combine DataFrame’s `isin` with the `any()` and `all()` methods to
quickly select subsets of your data that meet a given criteria.
To select a row where each column meets its own criterion:

```
In [214]: values = {'ids': ['a', 'b'], 'ids2': ['a', 'c'], 'vals': [1, 3]}
In [215]: row_mask = df.isin(values).all(axis=1)
In [216]: df[row_mask]
Out[216]: 
   vals ids ids2
0     1   a    a
```
Selecting values from a Series with a boolean vector generally returns a
subset of the data. To guarantee that selection output has the same shape as
the original data, you can use the `where` method in `Series` and `DataFrame`.

To return only the selected rows:

```
In [217]: s[s > 0]
Out[217]: 
3    1
2    2
1    3
0    4
dtype: int64
```
To return a Series of the same shape as the original:

```
In [218]: s.where(s > 0)
Out[218]: 
4    NaN
3    1.0
2    2.0
1    3.0
0    4.0
dtype: float64
```
Selecting values from a DataFrame with a boolean criterion now also preserves
input data shape. `where` is used under the hood as the implementation.
The code below is equivalent to `df.where(df < 0)`.

```

In [220]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 4),

```
In [229]: df.where(df < 0, -df) == np.where(df < 0, df, -df)

payload.content:
## Setting with enlargement conditionally using `numpy()`[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#setting-with-enlargement-conditionally-using-numpy)

An alternative to [`where()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.where.html#pandas.DataFrame.where) is to use [`numpy.where()`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.where.html#numpy.where).
Combined with setting a new column, you can use it to enlarge a DataFrame where the
values are determined conditionally.

Consider you have two choices to choose from in the following DataFrame. And you want to set a new column color to ‘green’ when the second column has ‘Z’. You can do the following:

```
In [241]: df = pd.DataFrame({'col1': list('ABBC'), 'col2': list('ZZXY')})
In [242]: df['color'] = np.where(df['col2'] == 'Z', 'green', 'red')
In [243]: df
Out[243]: 
  col1 col2  color
0    A    Z  green
1    B    Z  green
2    B    X    red
3    C    Y    red
```
If you have multiple conditions, you can use [`numpy.select()`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.select.html#numpy.select) to achieve that.  Say
corresponding to three conditions there are three choice of colors, with a fourth color
as a fallback, you can do the following.

```
In [244]: conditions = [
   .....:     (df['col2'] == 'Z') & (df['col1'] == 'A'),
   .....:     (df['col2'] == 'Z') & (df['col1'] == 'B'),
   .....:     (df['col1'] == 'B')
   .....: ]
   .....: 
In [245]: choices = ['yellow', 'blue', 'purple']
In [246]: df['color'] = np.select(conditions, choices, default='black')
In [247]: df
Out[247]: 
  col1 col2   color
0    A    Z  yellow
1    B    Z    blue
2    B    X  purple
3    C    Y   black
```

method that allows selection using an expression.

You can get the value of the frame where column `b` has values
between the values of columns `a` and `c`. For example:

```
In [248]: n = 10
In [249]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(n, 3), columns=list('abc'))
In [250]: df
Out[250]: 
          a         b         c
0  0.977227  0.727376  0.630865
1  0.076462  0.474453  0.438921

7  0.523211  0.591538  0.792342
8  0.216974  0.564056  0.397890
9  0.454131  0.915716  0.074315

payload.content:
## query

In [252]: df.query('(a < b) & (b < c)')
Out[252]: 
          a         b         c
7  0.523211  0.591538  0.792342
```
Do the same thing but fall back on a named index if there is no column
with the name `a`.

```
In [253]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randint(n / 2, size=(n, 2)), columns=list('bc'))
In [254]: df.index.name = 'a'
In [255]: df
Out[255]: 
   b  c
a      
0  0  0
1  3  1
2  3  4
3  0  4
4  0  1
5  3  4
6  4  3
7  1  4
8  0  3
9  0  1
In [256]: df.query('a < b and b < c')
Out[256]: 
   b  c
a      
2  3  4
```
If instead you don’t want to or cannot name your index, you can use the name
`index` in your query expression:

```
In [257]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randint(n, size=(n, 2)), columns=list('bc'))
In [258]: df
Out[258]: 
   b  c
0  2  3
1  9  1
2  3  1
3  3  0
4  5  6
5  5  2
6  7  4
7  0  1
8  2  5
9  0  1
In [259]: df.query('index < b < c')
Out[259]: 
   b  c
0  2  3
4  5  6
```
Note

If the name of your index overlaps with a column name, the column name is given precedence. For example,

```
In [260]: df = pd.DataFrame({'a': np.random.randint(5, size=5)})
In [261]: df.index.name = 'a'
In [262]: df.query('a > 2')  # uses the column 'a', not the index
Out[262]: 
   a
a   
3  3
```
You can still use the index in a query expression by using the special identifier ‘index’:

```
In [263]: df.query('index > 2')
Out[263]: 
   a
a   
3  3
4  1
```
If for some reason you have a column named `index`, then you can refer to
the index as `ilevel_0` as well, but at this point you should consider
renaming your columns to something less ambiguous.

## [`MultiIndex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.MultiIndex.html#pandas.MultiIndex) [`query()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.query.html#pandas.DataFrame.query) Syntax[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#multiindex-query-syntax)

You can also use the levels of a `DataFrame` with a
[`MultiIndex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.MultiIndex.html#pandas.MultiIndex) as if they were columns in the frame:

```
In [264]: n = 10
In [265]: colors = np.random.choice(['red', 'green'], size=n)
In [266]: foods = np.random.choice(['eggs', 'ham'], size=n)
In [267]: colors
Out[267]: 
array(['green', 'green', 'red', 'green', 'red', 'red', 'red', 'red',
       'green', 'green'], dtype='<U5')
In [268]: foods
Out[268]: 
array(['ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham', 'eggs', 'eggs',
       'eggs'], dtype='<U4')
In [269]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([colors, foods], names=['color', 'food'])
In [270]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(n, 2), index=index)
In [271]: df
Out[271]:

be evaluated using `numexpr` will be.

## Duplicate data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#duplicate-data)

If you want to identify and remove duplicate rows in a DataFrame,  there are
two methods that will help: `duplicated` and `drop_duplicates`. Each
takes as an argument the columns to use to identify duplicated rows.

- `duplicated` returns a boolean vector whose length is the number of rows, and which indicates whether a row is duplicated.
- `drop_duplicates` removes duplicate rows.

By default, the first observed row of a duplicate set is considered unique, but
each method has a `keep` parameter to specify targets to be kept.

- `keep='first'` (default): mark / drop duplicates except for the first occurrence.
- `keep='last'`: mark / drop duplicates except for the last occurrence.
- `keep=False`: mark  / drop all duplicates.

```
In [316]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({'a': ['one', 'one', 'two', 'two', 'two', 'three', 'four'],
   .....:                     'b': ['x', 'y', 'x', 'y', 'x', 'x', 'x'],
   .....:                     'c': np.random.randn(7)})
   .....: 
In [317]: df2
Out[317]: 
       a  b         c
0    one  x -1.467157
1    one  y  0.113937
2    two  x -1.428572
3    two  y  0.337109
4    two  x  0.052469
5  three  x -2.294560
6   four  x  2.148507
In [318]: df2.duplicated('a')
Out[318]: 
0    False
1     True
2    False
3     True
4     True
5    False
6    False
dtype: bool
In [319]: df2.duplicated('a', keep='last')
Out[319]: 
0     True
1    False
2     True
3     True
4    False
5    False
6    False
dtype: bool
In [320]: df2.duplicated('a', keep=False)
Out[320]: 
0     True
1     True
2     True
3     True
4     True
5    False
6    False
dtype: bool
In [321]: df2.drop_duplicates('a')
Out[321]: 
       a  b         c
0    one  x -1.467157
2    two  x -1.428572
5  three  x -2.294560

payload.content:
## Looking up values by index/column labels[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#looking-up-values-by-index-column-labels)

Sometimes you want to extract a set of values given a sequence of row labels
and column labels, this can be achieved by `pandas.factorize`  and NumPy indexing.

For heterogeneous column types, we subset columns to avoid unnecessary NumPy conversions:

```
def pd_lookup_het(df, row_labels, col_labels):
   rows = df.index.get_indexer(row_labels)
   cols = df.columns.get_indexer(col_labels)
   sub = df.take(np.unique(cols), axis=1)
   sub = sub.take(np.unique(rows), axis=0)
   rows = sub.index.get_indexer(row_labels)
   values = sub.melt()["value"]
   cols = sub.columns.get_indexer(col_labels)
   flat_index = rows + cols * len(sub)
   result = values[flat_index]
   return result
```
For homogeneous column types, it is fastest to skip column subsetting and go directly to NumPy:

```
def pd_lookup_hom(df, row_labels, col_labels):
    rows = df.index.get_indexer(row_labels)
    df = df.loc[:, sorted(set(col_labels))]
    cols = df.columns.get_indexer(col_labels)
    result = df.to_numpy()[rows, cols]
    return result
```
Formerly this could be achieved with the dedicated `DataFrame.lookup` method
which was deprecated in version 1.2.0 and removed in version 2.0.0.

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Index objects[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#index-objects)
payload.content:
## Index objects[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#index-objects)

The pandas [`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index) class and its subclasses can be viewed as
implementing an *ordered multiset*. Duplicates are allowed.

[`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index) also provides the infrastructure necessary for
lookups, data alignment, and reindexing. The easiest way to create an
[`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index) directly is to pass a `list` or other sequence to
[`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index):

```
In [335]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'])
In [336]: index
Out[336]: Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype='str')
In [337]: 'd' in index
Out[337]: True
```
or using numbers:

```
In [338]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12])
In [339]: index
Out[339]: Index([1, 5, 12], dtype='int64')
In [340]: 5 in index
Out[340]: True
```
If no dtype is given, `Index` tries to infer the dtype from the data.
It is also possible to give an explicit dtype when instantiating an [`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index):

```
In [341]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype="string")
In [342]: index
Out[342]: Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], dtype='string')
In [343]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12], dtype="int8")
In [344]: index
Out[344]: Index([1, 5, 12], dtype='int8')
In [345]: index = pd.Index([1, 5, 12], dtype="float32")
In [346]: index
Out[346]: Index([1.0, 5.0, 12.0], dtype='float32')
```
You can also pass a `name` to be stored in the index:

```
In [347]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], name='something')
In [348]: index.name
Out[348]: 'something'
```

In [347]: index = pd.Index(['e', 'd', 'a', 'b'], name='something')

payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Setting metadata[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#setting-metadata)
payload.content:
## Setting metadata[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#setting-metadata)

Indexes are “mostly immutable”, but it is possible to set and change their
`name` attribute. You can use the `rename`, `set_names` to set these attributes
directly, and they default to returning a copy.

See [Advanced Indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced) for usage of MultiIndexes.

```
In [354]: ind = pd.Index([1, 2, 3])
In [355]: ind.rename("apple")
Out[355]: Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64', name='apple')
In [356]: ind
Out[356]: Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64')
In [357]: ind = ind.set_names(["apple"])
In [358]: ind.name = "bob"
In [359]: ind
Out[359]: Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64', name='bob')
```
`set_names`, `set_levels`, and `set_codes` also take an optional
`level` argument

```
In [360]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([range(3), ['one', 'two']], names=['first', 'second'])
In [361]: index
Out[361]: 
MultiIndex([(0, 'one'),
            (0, 'two'),
            (1, 'one'),
            (1, 'two'),
            (2, 'one'),
            (2, 'two')],
           names=['first', 'second'])
In [362]: index.levels[1]
Out[362]: Index(['one', 'two'], dtype='str', name='second')
In [363]: index.set_levels(["a", "b"], level=1)
Out[363]: 
MultiIndex([(0, 'a'),
            (0, 'b'),
            (1, 'a'),
            (1, 'b'),
            (2, 'a'),
            (2, 'b')],
           names=['first', 'second'])
```

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Set operations on Index objects[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#set-operations-on-index-objects)
payload.content:
## Set operations on Index objects[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#set-operations-on-index-objects)

The two main operations are `union` and `intersection`.
Difference is provided via the `.difference()` method.

```
In [364]: a = pd.Index(['c', 'b', 'a'])
In [365]: b = pd.Index(['c', 'e', 'd'])
In [366]: a.difference(b)
Out[366]: Index(['a', 'b'], dtype='str')
```
Also available is the `symmetric_difference` operation, which returns elements
that appear in either `idx1` or `idx2`, but not in both. This is
equivalent to the Index created by `idx1.difference(idx2).union(idx2.difference(idx1))`,
with duplicates dropped.

```
In [367]: idx1 = pd.Index([1, 2, 3, 4])
In [368]: idx2 = pd.Index([2, 3, 4, 5])
In [369]: idx1.symmetric_difference(idx2)
Out[369]: Index([1, 5], dtype='int64')
```
Note

The resulting index from a set operation will be sorted in ascending order.

When performing [`Index.union()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.union.html#pandas.Index.union) between indexes with different dtypes, the indexes
must be cast to a common dtype. Typically, though not always, this is object dtype. The
exception is when performing a union between integer and float data. In this case, the
integer values are converted to float

```
In [370]: idx1 = pd.Index([0, 1, 2])
In [371]: idx2 = pd.Index([0.5, 1.5])
In [372]: idx1.union(idx2)
Out[372]: Index([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0], dtype='float64')
```

payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Missing values[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#missing-values)
payload.content:
## Missing values[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#missing-values)

Important

Even though `Index` can hold missing values (`NaN`), it should be avoided
if you do not want any unexpected results. For example, some operations
exclude missing values implicitly.

`Index.fillna` fills missing values with specified scalar value.

```
In [373]: idx1 = pd.Index([1, np.nan, 3, 4])
In [374]: idx1
Out[374]: Index([1.0, nan, 3.0, 4.0], dtype='float64')
In [375]: idx1.fillna(2)
Out[375]: Index([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], dtype='float64')
In [376]: idx2 = pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp('2011-01-01'),
   .....:                          pd.NaT,
   .....:                          pd.Timestamp('2011-01-03')])
   .....: 
In [377]: idx2
Out[377]: 
DatetimeIndex(['2011-01-01', 'NaT', '2011-01-03'], dtype='datetime64[us]',
              freq=None)
In [378]: idx2.fillna(pd.Timestamp('2011-01-02'))
Out[378]: 
DatetimeIndex(['2011-01-01', '2011-01-02', '2011-01-03'],
              dtype='datetime64[us]', freq=None)
```

payload.content:
## Set / reset index[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#set-reset-index)

Occasionally you will load or create a data set into a DataFrame and want to add an index after you’ve already done so. There are a couple of different ways.

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Set an index[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#set-an-index)
payload.content:
## Set an index[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#set-an-index)

DataFrame has a [`set_index()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.set_index.html#pandas.DataFrame.set_index) method which takes a column name
(for a regular `Index`) or a list of column names (for a `MultiIndex`).
To create a new, re-indexed DataFrame:

```
In [379]: data = pd.DataFrame({'a': ['bar', 'bar', 'foo', 'foo'],
   .....:                      'b': ['one', 'two', 'one', 'two'],
   .....:                      'c': ['z', 'y', 'x', 'w'],
   .....:                      'd': [1., 2., 3, 4]})
   .....: 
In [380]: data
Out[380]: 
     a    b  c    d
0  bar  one  z  1.0
1  bar  two  y  2.0
2  foo  one  x  3.0
3  foo  two  w  4.0
In [381]: indexed1 = data.set_index('c')
In [382]: indexed1
Out[382]: 
     a    b    d
c               
z  bar  one  1.0
y  bar  two  2.0
x  foo  one  3.0
w  foo  two  4.0
In [383]: indexed2 = data.set_index(['a', 'b'])
In [384]: indexed2
Out[384]: 
         c    d
a   b          
bar one  z  1.0
    two  y  2.0
foo one  x  3.0
    two  w  4.0
```
The `append` keyword option allow you to keep the existing index and append
the given columns to a MultiIndex:

```
In [385]: frame = data.set_index('c', drop=False)
In [386]: frame = frame.set_index(['a', 'b'], append=True)
In [387]: frame
Out[387]: 
           c    d
c a   b          
z bar one  z  1.0
y bar two  y  2.0
x foo one  x  3.0
w foo two  w  4.0
```
Other options in `set_index` allow you not drop the index columns.

```
In [388]: data.set_index('c', drop=False)
Out[388]: 
     a    b  c    d
c                  
z  bar  one  z  1.0
y  bar  two  y  2.0
x  foo  one  x  3.0
w  foo  two  w  4.0
```

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Reset the index[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#reset-the-index)
payload.content:
## Reset the index[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#reset-the-index)

As a convenience, there is a new function on DataFrame called
[`reset_index()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.reset_index.html#pandas.DataFrame.reset_index) which transfers the index values into the
DataFrame’s columns and sets a simple integer index.
This is the inverse operation of [`set_index()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.set_index.html#pandas.DataFrame.set_index).

```
In [389]: data
Out[389]: 
     a    b  c    d
0  bar  one  z  1.0
1  bar  two  y  2.0
2  foo  one  x  3.0
3  foo  two  w  4.0
In [390]: data.reset_index()
Out[390]: 
   index    a    b  c    d
0      0  bar  one  z  1.0
1      1  bar  two  y  2.0
2      2  foo  one  x  3.0
3      3  foo  two  w  4.0
```
The output is more similar to a SQL table or a record array. The names for the
columns derived from the index are the ones stored in the `names` attribute.

You can use the `level` keyword to remove only a portion of the index:

```
In [391]: frame
Out[391]: 
           c    d
c a   b          
z bar one  z  1.0
y bar two  y  2.0
x foo one  x  3.0
w foo two  w  4.0
In [392]: frame.reset_index(level=1)
Out[392]: 
         a  c    d
c b               
z one  bar  z  1.0
y two  bar  y  2.0
x one  foo  x  3.0
w two  foo  w  4.0
```
`reset_index` takes an optional parameter `drop` which if true simply
discards the index, instead of putting index values in the DataFrame’s columns.

In [394]: df_idx.index = pd.Index([10, 20, 30, 40], name="a")
In [395]: df_idx
Out[395]:

a    
10  0

40  3
```

## Why does assignment fail when using chained indexing?[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#why-does-assignment-fail-when-using-chained-indexing)

[Copy-on-Write](https://pandas.pydata.org/migration.html#copy-on-write) is the new default with pandas 3.0.

for more context.

payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Series Assignment and Index Alignment[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series-assignment-and-index-alignment)
payload.content:
## Series Assignment and Index Alignment[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#series-assignment-and-index-alignment)

When assigning a Series to a DataFrame column, pandas performs automatic alignment based on index labels. This is a fundamental behavior that can be surprising to new users who might expect positional assignment.

payload.title: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Key Points:[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#key-points)
payload.content:
## Key Points:[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#key-points)

- Series values are matched to DataFrame rows by index label
- Position/order in the Series doesn’t matter
- Missing index labels result in NaN values
- This behavior is consistent across df\[col\] = series and df.loc\[:, col\] = series

You can think of this as reindexing the Series to the DataFrame index before
assignment (for example, `df[col] = series.reindex(df.index)`).

Examples: .. ipython:: python

import pandas as pd

\# Create a DataFrame df = pd.DataFrame({‘values’: \[1, 2, 3\]}, index=\[‘x’, ‘y’, ‘z’\])

\# Series with matching indices (different order) s1 = pd.Series(\[10, 20, 30\], index=\[‘z’, ‘x’, ‘y’\]) df\[‘aligned’\] = s1 # Aligns by index, not position print(df)

\# Series with partial index match s2 = pd.Series(\[100, 200\], index=\[‘x’, ‘z’\]) df\[‘partial’\] = s2 # Missing ‘y’ gets NaN print(df)

\# Series with non-matching indices s3 = pd.Series(\[1000, 2000\], index=\[‘a’, ‘b’\]) df\[‘nomatch’\] = s3 # All values become NaN print(df)

#Avoiding Confusion: #If you want positional assignment instead of index alignment: # reset the Series index to match DataFrame index df\[‘s1\_values’\] = s1.reindex(df.index)

payload.breadcrumb: Indexing and selecting data — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > equivalent in pure Python > Column assignment vs. in-place setting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#column-assignment-vs-in-place-setting)
payload.content:
## Column assignment vs. in-place setting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#column-assignment-vs-in-place-setting)

While index alignment is consistent between `df[col] = value` and
`df.loc[:, col] = value` (see the previous section), the two forms differ in
how they treat the column’s existing dtype:

- `df[col] = value` **replaces** the column. The new column’s dtype is
inferred from `value`, regardless of what dtype the old column had.
- `df.loc[:, col] = value` (and `df.iloc[:, i] = value`) **sets the values
in place** in the existing column. The original dtype is preserved, and the
assignment will raise `TypeError` if `value` is not compatible with it.

This is most visible for `ExtensionDtype` columns
such as `category`, `Int64`, `boolean`, or `string`, where the
replacing form silently drops the extension dtype:

```
In [396]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.Categorical(["x", "y"], categories=["x", "y", "z"])})
In [397]: df["a"] = "z"          # replaces the column
In [398]: df.dtypes
Out[398]: 
a    str
dtype: object
In [399]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.Categorical(["x", "y"], categories=["x", "y", "z"])})
In [400]: df.loc[:, "a"] = "z"   # sets values in place
In [401]: df.dtypes
Out[401]: 
a    category
dtype: object
```
The same distinction applies to nullable numeric and boolean dtypes:

```
In [402]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.array([1, 2], dtype="Int64")})
In [403]: df["a"] = 5
In [404]: df.dtypes
Out[404]: 
a    int64
dtype: object
In [405]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.array([1, 2], dtype="Int64")})
In [406]: df.loc[:, "a"] = 5
In [407]: df.dtypes
Out[407]: 
a    Int64
dtype: object
```
Use `df.loc[:, col] = value` (or `.iloc`) when you want to update every
value of an existing column while keeping its dtype.

Use [`DataFrame.head()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html#pandas.DataFrame.head) and [`DataFrame.tail()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.tail.html#pandas.DataFrame.tail) to view the top and bottom rows of the frame

Out[14]: 
                   A         B         C         D
2013-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771 -1.039575  0.271860

2013-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648 -1.478427  0.524988

DatetimeIndex(['2013-01-01', '2013-01-02', '2013-01-03', '2013-01-04',

## Selection[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selection)

Note

While standard Python / NumPy expressions for selecting and setting are
intuitive and come in handy for interactive work, for production code, we
recommend the optimized pandas data access methods, [`DataFrame.at`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.at.html#pandas.DataFrame.at), [`DataFrame.iat`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.iat.html#pandas.DataFrame.iat),
[`DataFrame.loc()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.loc.html#pandas.DataFrame.loc) and [`DataFrame.iloc()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.iloc.html#pandas.DataFrame.iloc).

See the indexing documentation [Indexing and Selecting Data](https://pandas.pydata.org/indexing.html#indexing) and [MultiIndex / Advanced Indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/advanced.html#advanced).

payload.content:
## Getitem (`[]`)[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#getitem)

For a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame), passing a single label selects a column and
yields a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series):

```
In [24]: df["A"]
Out[24]: 
2013-01-01    0.469112
2013-01-02    1.212112
2013-01-03   -0.861849
2013-01-04    0.721555
2013-01-05   -0.424972
2013-01-06   -0.673690
Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64
```
If the label only contains letters, numbers, and underscores, you can alternatively use the column name attribute:

```
In [25]: df.A
Out[25]: 
2013-01-01    0.469112
2013-01-02    1.212112
2013-01-03   -0.861849
2013-01-04    0.721555
2013-01-05   -0.424972
2013-01-06   -0.673690
Freq: D, Name: A, dtype: float64
```
Passing a list of column labels selects multiple columns, which can be useful for getting a subset/rearranging:

```
In [26]: df[["B", "A"]]
Out[26]: 
                   B         A
2013-01-01 -0.282863  0.469112
2013-01-02 -0.173215  1.212112
2013-01-03 -2.104569 -0.861849
2013-01-04 -0.706771  0.721555
2013-01-05  0.567020 -0.424972
2013-01-06  0.113648 -0.673690
```
For a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame), passing a slice `:` selects matching rows:

```
In [27]: df[0:3]
Out[27]: 
                   A         B         C         D
2013-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863 -1.509059 -1.135632
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  1.071804
In [28]: df["20130102":"20130104"]
Out[28]: 
                   A         B         C         D
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  1.071804

payload.content:
## Selection by label[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selection-by-label)

See more in [Selection by Label](https://pandas.pydata.org/indexing.html#indexing-label) using [`DataFrame.loc()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.loc.html#pandas.DataFrame.loc) or [`DataFrame.at`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.at.html#pandas.DataFrame.at).

Selecting a row matching a label:

```
In [29]: df.loc[dates[0]]
Out[29]: 
A    0.469112
B   -0.282863
C   -1.509059
D   -1.135632
Name: 2013-01-01 00:00:00, dtype: float64
```
Selecting all rows (`:`) with a select column labels:

```
In [30]: df.loc[:, ["A", "B"]]
Out[30]: 
                   A         B
2013-01-01  0.469112 -0.282863
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
2013-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
2013-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
2013-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648
```
For label slicing, both endpoints are *included*:

```
In [31]: df.loc["20130102":"20130104", ["A", "B"]]
Out[31]: 
                   A         B
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569
2013-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
```
Selecting a single row and column label returns a scalar:

```
In [32]: df.loc[dates[0], "A"]
Out[32]: np.float64(0.4691122999071863)
```
For getting fast access to a scalar (equivalent to the prior method):

```
In [33]: df.at[dates[0], "A"]
Out[33]: np.float64(0.4691122999071863)
```

payload.content:
## Selection by position[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#selection-by-position)

See more in [Selection by Position](https://pandas.pydata.org/indexing.html#indexing-integer) using [`DataFrame.iloc()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.iloc.html#pandas.DataFrame.iloc) or [`DataFrame.iat`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.iat.html#pandas.DataFrame.iat).

Select via the position of the passed integers:

```
In [34]: df.iloc[3]
Out[34]: 
A    0.721555
B   -0.706771
C   -1.039575
D    0.271860
Name: 2013-01-04 00:00:00, dtype: float64
```
Integer slices act similar to NumPy/Python:

```
In [35]: df.iloc[3:5, 0:2]
Out[35]: 
                   A         B
2013-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771
2013-01-05 -0.424972  0.567020
```
Lists of integer position locations:

```
In [36]: df.iloc[[1, 2, 4], [0, 2]]
Out[36]: 
                   A         C
2013-01-02  1.212112  0.119209
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -0.494929
2013-01-05 -0.424972  0.276232
```
For slicing rows explicitly:

```
In [37]: df.iloc[1:3, :]
Out[37]: 
                   A         B         C         D
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  1.071804
```
For slicing columns explicitly:

```
In [38]: df.iloc[:, 1:3]
Out[38]: 
                   B         C
2013-01-01 -0.282863 -1.509059
2013-01-02 -0.173215  0.119209
2013-01-03 -2.104569 -0.494929
2013-01-04 -0.706771 -1.039575
2013-01-05  0.567020  0.276232
2013-01-06  0.113648 -1.478427
```
For getting a value explicitly:

```
In [39]: df.iloc[1, 1]
Out[39]: np.float64(-0.17321464905330858)
```
For getting fast access to a scalar (equivalent to the prior method):

```
In [40]: df.iat[1, 1]
Out[40]: np.float64(-0.17321464905330858)
```

payload.content:
## Missing data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#missing-data)

For NumPy data types, `np.nan` represents missing data. It is by
default not included in computations. See the [Missing Data section](https://pandas.pydata.org/missing_data.html#missing-data).

Reindexing allows you to change/add/delete the index on a specified axis. This returns a copy of the data:

```
In [57]: df1 = df.reindex(index=dates[0:4], columns=list(df.columns) + ["E"])
In [58]: df1.loc[dates[0] : dates[1], "E"] = 1
In [59]: df1
Out[59]: 
                   A         B         C    D    F    E
2013-01-01  0.000000  0.000000 -1.509059  5.0  NaN  1.0
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209  5.0  1.0  1.0
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  5.0  2.0  NaN
2013-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771 -1.039575  5.0  3.0  NaN
```
[`DataFrame.dropna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.dropna.html#pandas.DataFrame.dropna) drops any rows that have missing data:

```
In [60]: df1.dropna(how="any")
Out[60]: 
                   A         B         C    D    F    E
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209  5.0  1.0  1.0
```
[`DataFrame.fillna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.fillna.html#pandas.DataFrame.fillna) fills missing data:

```
In [61]: df1.fillna(value=5)
Out[61]: 
                   A         B         C    D    F    E
2013-01-01  0.000000  0.000000 -1.509059  5.0  5.0  1.0
2013-01-02  1.212112 -0.173215  0.119209  5.0  1.0  1.0
2013-01-03 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929  5.0  2.0  5.0
2013-01-04  0.721555 -0.706771 -1.039575  5.0  3.0  5.0
```
[`isna()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.isna.html#pandas.isna) gets the boolean mask where values are `nan`:

```
In [62]: pd.isna(df1)
Out[62]: 
                A      B      C      D      F      E

payload.content:
## Stats[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#stats)

Operations in general *exclude* missing data.

Calculate the mean value for each column:

```
In [63]: df.mean()
Out[63]: 
A   -0.004474
B   -0.383981
C   -0.687758
D    5.000000
F    3.000000
dtype: float64
```
Calculate the mean value for each row:

```
In [64]: df.mean(axis=1)
Out[64]: 
2013-01-01    0.872735
2013-01-02    1.431621
2013-01-03    0.707731
2013-01-04    1.395042
2013-01-05    1.883656
2013-01-06    1.592306
Freq: D, dtype: float64
```
Operating with another [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) or [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) with a different index or column
will align the result with the union of the index or column labels. In addition, pandas
automatically broadcasts along the specified dimension and will fill unaligned labels with `np.nan`.

```
In [65]: s = pd.Series([1, 3, 5, np.nan, 6, 8], index=dates).shift(2)
In [66]: s
Out[66]: 
2013-01-01    NaN
2013-01-02    NaN
2013-01-03    1.0
2013-01-04    3.0
2013-01-05    5.0
2013-01-06    NaN
Freq: D, dtype: float64
In [67]: df.sub(s, axis="index")
Out[67]: 
                   A         B         C    D    F
2013-01-01       NaN       NaN       NaN  NaN  NaN
2013-01-02       NaN       NaN       NaN  NaN  NaN
2013-01-03 -1.861849 -3.104569 -1.494929  4.0  1.0
2013-01-04 -2.278445 -3.706771 -4.039575  2.0  0.0
2013-01-05 -5.424972 -4.432980 -4.723768  0.0 -1.0
2013-01-06       NaN       NaN       NaN  NaN  NaN
```

## User defined functions[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#user-defined-functions)

[`DataFrame.agg()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.agg.html#pandas.DataFrame.agg) and [`DataFrame.transform()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.transform.html#pandas.DataFrame.transform) applies a user defined function
that reduces or broadcasts its result respectively.

```
In [68]: df.agg(lambda x: np.mean(x) * 5.6)
Out[68]:

C    -3.851445
D    28.000000
F    16.800000
dtype: float64
In [69]: df.transform(lambda x: x * 101.2)
Out[69]:

2013-01-03  -87.219115 -212.982405  -50.086843  506.0  202.4

2013-01-05  -43.007200   57.382459   27.954680  506.0  404.8

## String Methods[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#string-methods)

[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) is equipped with a set of string processing methods in the `str`
attribute that make it easy to operate on each element of the array, as in the
code snippet below. See more at [Vectorized String Methods](https://pandas.pydata.org/text.html#text-string-methods).

```
In [73]: s = pd.Series(["A", "B", "C", "Aaba", "Baca", np.nan, "CABA", "dog", "cat"])
In [74]: s.str.lower()
Out[74]: 
0       a
1       b
2       c
3    aaba
4    baca
5     NaN
6    caba
7     dog
8     cat
dtype: str
```

## Concat[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#concat)

pandas provides various facilities for easily combining together [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) and
[`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) objects with various kinds of set logic for the indexes
and relational algebra functionality in the case of join / merge-type
operations.

See the [Merging section](https://pandas.pydata.org/merging.html#merging).

Concatenating pandas objects together row-wise with [`concat()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.concat.html#pandas.concat):

```
In [75]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(10, 4))
In [76]: df

payload.content:
## Join[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#join)

[`merge()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.merge.html#pandas.merge) enables SQL style join types along specific columns. See the [Database style joining](https://pandas.pydata.org/merging.html#merging-join) section.

```
In [79]: left = pd.DataFrame({"key": ["foo", "foo"], "lval": [1, 2]})
In [80]: right = pd.DataFrame({"key": ["foo", "foo"], "rval": [4, 5]})
In [81]: left
Out[81]: 
   key  lval
0  foo     1
1  foo     2
In [82]: right
Out[82]: 
   key  rval
0  foo     4
1  foo     5
In [83]: pd.merge(left, right, on="key")
Out[83]: 
   key  lval  rval
0  foo     1     4
1  foo     1     5
2  foo     2     4
3  foo     2     5
```
[`merge()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.merge.html#pandas.merge) on unique keys:

```
In [84]: left = pd.DataFrame({"key": ["foo", "bar"], "lval": [1, 2]})
In [85]: right = pd.DataFrame({"key": ["foo", "bar"], "rval": [4, 5]})
In [86]: left
Out[86]: 
   key  lval
0  foo     1
1  bar     2
In [87]: right
Out[87]: 
   key  rval
0  foo     4
1  bar     5
In [88]: pd.merge(left, right, on="key")
Out[88]: 
   key  lval  rval
0  foo     1     4
1  bar     2     5
```

payload.content:
## Grouping[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#grouping)

By “group by” we are referring to a process involving one or more of the following steps:

- **Splitting** the data into groups based on some criteria
- **Applying** a function to each group independently
- **Combining** the results into a data structure

See the [Grouping section](https://pandas.pydata.org/groupby.html#groupby).

```
In [89]: df = pd.DataFrame(
   ....:     {
   ....:         "A": ["foo", "bar", "foo", "bar", "foo", "bar", "foo", "foo"],
   ....:         "B": ["one", "one", "two", "three", "two", "two", "one", "three"],
   ....:         "C": np.random.randn(8),
   ....:         "D": np.random.randn(8),
   ....:     }
   ....: )
   ....: 
In [90]: df
Out[90]: 
     A      B         C         D
0  foo    one  1.346061 -1.577585
1  bar    one  1.511763  0.396823
2  foo    two  1.627081 -0.105381
3  bar  three -0.990582 -0.532532
4  foo    two -0.441652  1.453749
5  bar    two  1.211526  1.208843
6  foo    one  0.268520 -0.080952
7  foo  three  0.024580 -0.264610
```
Grouping by a column label, selecting column labels, and then applying the
[`DataFrameGroupBy.sum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.typing.DataFrameGroupBy.sum.html#pandas.api.typing.DataFrameGroupBy.sum) function to the resulting
groups:

```
In [91]: df.groupby("A")[["C", "D"]].sum()
Out[91]: 
            C         D
A                      
bar  1.732707  1.073134
foo  2.824590 -0.574779
```
The unique values of the grouped column now form the index of the result.

Grouping by multiple columns label forms [`MultiIndex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.MultiIndex.html#pandas.MultiIndex).

```
In [92]: df.groupby(["A", "B"]).sum()
Out[92]: 
                  C         D
A   B

payload.content:
## Stack[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#stack)

```
In [93]: arrays = [
   ....:    ["bar", "bar", "baz", "baz", "foo", "foo", "qux", "qux"],
   ....:    ["one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two", "one", "two"],
   ....: ]
   ....: 
In [94]: index = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays(arrays, names=["first", "second"])
In [95]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 2), index=index, columns=["A", "B"])
In [96]: df2 = df[:4]
In [97]: df2
Out[97]: 
                     A         B
first second                    
bar   one    -0.727965 -0.589346
      two     0.339969 -0.693205
baz   one    -0.339355  0.593616
      two     0.884345  1.591431
```
The [`stack()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.stack.html#pandas.DataFrame.stack) method “compresses” a level in the DataFrame’s
columns:

```
In [98]: stacked = df2.stack()
In [99]: stacked
Out[99]: 
first  second   
bar    one     A   -0.727965
               B   -0.589346
       two     A    0.339969
               B   -0.693205
baz    one     A   -0.339355
               B    0.593616
       two     A    0.884345
               B    1.591431
dtype: float64
```
With a “stacked” DataFrame or Series (having a [`MultiIndex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.MultiIndex.html#pandas.MultiIndex) as the
`index`), the inverse operation of [`stack()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.stack.html#pandas.DataFrame.stack) is
[`unstack()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.unstack.html#pandas.DataFrame.unstack), which by default unstacks the **last level**:

```
In [100]: stacked.unstack()
Out[100]: 
                     A         B
first second                    
bar   one    -0.727965 -0.589346
      two     0.339969 -0.693205
baz   one    -0.339355  0.593616

   .....:         "C": ["foo", "foo", "foo", "bar", "bar", "bar"] * 2,
   .....:         "D": np.random.randn(12),
   .....:         "E": np.random.randn(12),
   .....:     }
   .....: )
   .....:

Out[104]: 
        A  B    C         D         E
0     one  A  foo -1.202872  0.047609

payload.content:
## Time series[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#time-series)

pandas has simple, powerful, and efficient functionality for performing
resampling operations during frequency conversion (e.g., converting secondly
data into 5-minutely data). This is extremely common in, but not limited to,
financial applications. See the [Time Series section](https://pandas.pydata.org/timeseries.html#timeseries).

```
In [106]: rng = pd.date_range("1/1/2012", periods=100, freq="s")
In [107]: ts = pd.Series(np.random.randint(0, 500, len(rng)), index=rng)
In [108]: ts.resample("5Min").sum()
Out[108]: 
2012-01-01    24182
Freq: 5min, dtype: int64
```
[`Series.tz_localize()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.tz_localize.html#pandas.Series.tz_localize) localizes a time series to a time zone:

```
In [109]: rng = pd.date_range("3/6/2012 00:00", periods=5, freq="D")
In [110]: ts = pd.Series(np.random.randn(len(rng)), rng)
In [111]: ts
Out[111]: 
2012-03-06    1.857704
2012-03-07   -1.193545
2012-03-08    0.677510
2012-03-09   -0.153931
2012-03-10    0.520091
Freq: D, dtype: float64
In [112]: ts_utc = ts.tz_localize("UTC")
In [113]: ts_utc
Out[113]: 
2012-03-06 00:00:00+00:00    1.857704
2012-03-07 00:00:00+00:00   -1.193545
2012-03-08 00:00:00+00:00    0.677510
2012-03-09 00:00:00+00:00   -0.153931
2012-03-10 00:00:00+00:00    0.520091
Freq: D, dtype: float64
```
[`Series.tz_convert()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.tz_convert.html#pandas.Series.tz_convert) converts a timezone aware time series to another time zone:

```
In [114]: ts_utc.tz_convert("US/Eastern")
Out[114]: 
2012-03-05 19:00:00-05:00    1.857704
2012-03-06 19:00:00-05:00   -1.193545
2012-03-07 19:00:00-05:00    0.677510
2012-03-08 19:00:00-05:00   -0.153931

payload.content:
## Categoricals[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#categoricals)

pandas can include categorical data in a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame). For full docs, see the
[categorical introduction](https://pandas.pydata.org/categorical.html#categorical) and the [API documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/arrays.html#api-arrays-categorical).

```
In [117]: df = pd.DataFrame(
   .....:     {"id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "raw_grade": ["a", "b", "b", "a", "a", "e"]}
   .....: )
   .....: 
```
Converting the raw grades to a categorical data type:

```
In [118]: df["grade"] = df["raw_grade"].astype("category")
In [119]: df["grade"]
Out[119]: 
0    a
1    b
2    b
3    a
4    a
5    e
Name: grade, dtype: category
Categories (3, str): ['a', 'b', 'e']
```
Rename the categories to more meaningful names:

```
In [120]: new_categories = ["very good", "good", "very bad"]
In [121]: df["grade"] = df["grade"].cat.rename_categories(new_categories)
```
Reorder the categories and simultaneously add the missing categories (methods under [`Series.cat()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.cat.html#pandas.Series.cat) return a new [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) by default):

```
In [122]: df["grade"] = df["grade"].cat.set_categories(
   .....:     ["very bad", "bad", "medium", "good", "very good"]
   .....: )
   .....: 
In [123]: df["grade"]
Out[123]: 
0    very good
1         good
2         good
3    very good
4    very good
5     very bad
Name: grade, dtype: category
Categories (5, str): ['very bad', 'bad', 'medium', 'good', 'very good']
```
Sorting is per order in the categories, not lexical order:

```
In [124]: df.sort_values(by="grade")
Out[124]:

payload.content:
## Plotting[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#plotting)

See the [Plotting](https://pandas.pydata.org/visualization.html#visualization) docs.

We use the standard convention for referencing the matplotlib API:

```
In [126]: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
In [127]: plt.close("all")
```
The `plt.close` method is used to [close](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.close.html) a figure window:

```
In [128]: ts = pd.Series(np.random.randn(1000), index=pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=1000))
In [129]: ts = ts.cumsum()
In [130]: ts.plot();
```
Note

When using Jupyter, the plot will appear using [`plot()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.plot.html#pandas.Series.plot).  Otherwise use
[matplotlib.pyplot.show](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.show.html) to show it or
[matplotlib.pyplot.savefig](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.savefig.html) to write it to a file.

[`plot()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.plot.html#pandas.DataFrame.plot) plots all columns:

```
In [131]: df = pd.DataFrame(
   .....:     np.random.randn(1000, 4), index=ts.index, columns=["A", "B", "C", "D"]
   .....: )
   .....: 
In [132]: df = df.cumsum()
In [133]: plt.figure();
In [134]: df.plot();
In [135]: plt.legend(loc='best');
```

## Parquet[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#parquet)

Writing to a Parquet file:

```

## Gotchas[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#gotchas)

If you are attempting to perform a boolean operation on a [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series) or [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame)
you might see an exception like:

```
In [143]: if pd.Series([False, True, False]):
   .....:      print("I was true")
   .....: 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[143], line 1
----> 1 if pd.Series([False, True, False]):
      2      print("I was true")
File ~/work/pandas/pandas/pandas/core/generic.py:1445, in NDFrame.__bool__(self)
   1443     @final
   1444     def __bool__(self) -> NoReturn:
-> 1445         raise ValueError(
   1446             f"The truth value of a {type(self).__name__} is ambiguous. "
   1447             "Use a.empty, a.item(), a.any() or a.all()."
   1448         )
ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous. Use a.empty, a.item(), a.any() or a.all().
```
See [Comparisons](https://pandas.pydata.org/basics.html#basics-compare) and [Gotchas](https://pandas.pydata.org/gotchas.html#gotchas) for an explanation and what to do.

payload.content:
## Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality)

Here we discuss a lot of the essential functionality common to the pandas data
structures. To begin, let’s create some example objects like we did in
the [10 minutes to pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/10min.html#min) section:

```
In [1]: index = pd.date_range("1/1/2000", periods=8)
In [2]: s = pd.Series(np.random.randn(5), index=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])
In [3]: df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(8, 3), index=index, columns=["A", "B", "C"])
```

payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Head and tail[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#head-and-tail)
payload.content:
## Head and tail[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#head-and-tail)

To view a small sample of a Series or DataFrame object, use the
[`head()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html#pandas.DataFrame.head) and [`tail()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.tail.html#pandas.DataFrame.tail) methods. The default number
of elements to display is five, but you may pass a custom number.

```
In [4]: long_series = pd.Series(np.random.randn(1000))
In [5]: long_series.head()
Out[5]: 
0   -1.157892
1   -1.344312
2    0.844885
3    1.075770
4   -0.109050
dtype: float64
In [6]: long_series.tail(3)
Out[6]: 
997   -0.289388
998   -1.020544
999    0.589993
dtype: float64
```

payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Attributes and underlying data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#attributes-and-underlying-data)
payload.content:
## Attributes and underlying data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#attributes-and-underlying-data)

pandas objects have a number of attributes enabling you to access the metadata.

- **shape**: gives the axis dimensions of the object, consistent with ndarray
  - Axis labels
    - **Series**: *index* (only axis)
    - **DataFrame**: *index* (rows) and *columns*

Note, **these attributes can be safely assigned to**!

```
In [7]: df[:2]
Out[7]: 
                   A         B         C
2000-01-01 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
2000-01-02 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929
In [8]: df.columns = [x.lower() for x in df.columns]
In [9]: df
Out[9]: 
                   a         b         c
2000-01-01 -0.173215  0.119209 -1.044236
2000-01-02 -0.861849 -2.104569 -0.494929
2000-01-03  1.071804  0.721555 -0.706771
2000-01-04 -1.039575  0.271860 -0.424972
2000-01-05  0.567020  0.276232 -1.087401
2000-01-06 -0.673690  0.113648 -1.478427
2000-01-07  0.524988  0.404705  0.577046
2000-01-08 -1.715002 -1.039268 -0.370647
```
pandas objects ([`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index), [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series), [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame)) can be
thought of as containers for arrays, which hold the actual data and do the
actual computation. For many types, the underlying array is a
[`numpy.ndarray`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html#numpy.ndarray). However, pandas and 3rd party libraries may *extend*
NumPy’s type system to add support for custom arrays
(see [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org#basics-dtypes)).

payload.title: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Attributes and underlying data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#attributes-and-underlying-data)
payload.content:
NumPy’s type system to add support for custom arrays
(see [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org#basics-dtypes)).

To get the actual data inside a [`Index`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Index.html#pandas.Index) or [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series), use
the `.array` property.

```
In [10]: s.array
Out[10]: 
<NumpyExtensionArray>
[ 0.4691122999071863, -0.2828633443286633, -1.5090585031735124,
 -1.1356323710171934,  1.2121120250208506]
Length: 5, dtype: float64
In [11]: s.index.array
Out[11]: 
<ArrowStringArray>
['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']
Length: 5, dtype: str
```
[`array`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.array.html#pandas.Series.array) will always be an [`ExtensionArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray).
The exact details of what an [`ExtensionArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray) is and why pandas uses them are a bit
beyond the scope of this introduction. See [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org#basics-dtypes) for more.

If you know you need a NumPy array, use [`to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.to_numpy.html#pandas.Series.to_numpy)
or `numpy.asarray()`.

```
In [12]: s.to_numpy()
Out[12]: array([ 0.4691, -0.2829, -1.5091, -1.1356,  1.2121])
In [13]: np.asarray(s)
Out[13]: array([ 0.4691, -0.2829, -1.5091, -1.1356,  1.2121])
```
When the Series or Index is backed by

payload.title: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Attributes and underlying data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#attributes-and-underlying-data)
payload.content:
or `numpy.asarray()`.

```
In [12]: s.to_numpy()
Out[12]: array([ 0.4691, -0.2829, -1.5091, -1.1356,  1.2121])
In [13]: np.asarray(s)
Out[13]: array([ 0.4691, -0.2829, -1.5091, -1.1356,  1.2121])
```
When the Series or Index is backed by
an [`ExtensionArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray), [`to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.to_numpy.html#pandas.Series.to_numpy)
may involve copying data and coercing values. See [dtypes](https://pandas.pydata.org#basics-dtypes) for more.

[`to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.to_numpy.html#pandas.Series.to_numpy) gives some control over the `dtype` of the
resulting [`numpy.ndarray`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html#numpy.ndarray). For example, consider datetimes with timezones.
NumPy doesn’t have a dtype to represent timezone-aware datetimes, so there
are two possibly useful representations:

1. An object-dtype [`numpy.ndarray`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html#numpy.ndarray) with [`Timestamp`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Timestamp.html#pandas.Timestamp) objects, each
with the correct `tz`.
2. A `datetime64[ns]` -dtype [`numpy.ndarray`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html#numpy.ndarray), where the values have
been converted to UTC and the timezone discarded.

Timezones may be preserved with `dtype=object`:

```
In [14]: ser = pd.Series(pd.date_range("2000", periods=2, tz="CET"))
In [15]: ser.to_numpy(dtype=object)
Out[15]: 
array([Timestamp('2000-01-01 00:00:00+0100', tz='CET'),
       Timestamp('2000-01-02 00:00:00+0100', tz='CET')], dtype=object)
```

payload.title: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Attributes and underlying data[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#attributes-and-underlying-data)
payload.content:
```
In [14]: ser = pd.Series(pd.date_range("2000", periods=2, tz="CET"))
In [15]: ser.to_numpy(dtype=object)
Out[15]: 
array([Timestamp('2000-01-01 00:00:00+0100', tz='CET'),
       Timestamp('2000-01-02 00:00:00+0100', tz='CET')], dtype=object)
```
Or thrown away with `dtype='datetime64[ns]'`:

```
In [16]: ser.to_numpy(dtype="datetime64[ns]")
Out[16]: 
array(['1999-12-31T23:00:00.000000000', '2000-01-01T23:00:00.000000000'],
      dtype='datetime64[ns]')
```
Getting the “raw data” inside a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame) is possibly a bit more
complex. When your `DataFrame` only has a single data type for all the
columns, [`DataFrame.to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.to_numpy.html#pandas.DataFrame.to_numpy) will return the underlying data:

```
In [17]: df.to_numpy()
Out[17]: 
array([[-0.1732,  0.1192, -1.0442],
       [-0.8618, -2.1046, -0.4949],
       [ 1.0718,  0.7216, -0.7068],
       [-1.0396,  0.2719, -0.425 ],
       [ 0.567 ,  0.2762, -1.0874],
       [-0.6737,  0.1136, -1.4784],
       [ 0.525 ,  0.4047,  0.577 ],
       [-1.715 , -1.0393, -0.3706]])
```
If a DataFrame contains homogeneously-typed data, the ndarray can actually be modified in-place, and the changes will be reflected in the data structure. For heterogeneous data (e.g. some of the DataFrame’s columns are not all the same dtype), this will not be the case. The values attribute itself, unlike the axis labels, cannot be assigned to.

Note

payload.content:
Note

When working with heterogeneous data, the dtype of the resulting ndarray will be chosen to accommodate all of the data involved. For example, if strings are involved, the result will be of object dtype. If there are only floats and integers, the resulting array will be of float dtype.

In the past, pandas recommended [`Series.values`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.values.html#pandas.Series.values) or [`DataFrame.values`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.values.html#pandas.DataFrame.values)
for extracting the data from a Series or DataFrame. You’ll still find references
to these in old code bases and online. Going forward, we recommend avoiding
`.values` and using `.array` or `.to_numpy()`. `.values` has the following
drawbacks:

1. When your Series contains an [extension type](https://pandas.pydata.org/development/extending.html#extending-extension-types), it’s
unclear whether [`Series.values`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.values.html#pandas.Series.values) returns a NumPy array or the extension array. [`Series.array`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.array.html#pandas.Series.array) will always return an [`ExtensionArray`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray.html#pandas.api.extensions.ExtensionArray), and will never
copy data. [`Series.to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.Series.to_numpy.html#pandas.Series.to_numpy) will always return a NumPy array,
potentially at the cost of copying / coercing values.
2. When your DataFrame contains a mixture of data types, [`DataFrame.values`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.values.html#pandas.DataFrame.values) may

payload.content:
potentially at the cost of copying / coercing values.
2. When your DataFrame contains a mixture of data types, [`DataFrame.values`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.values.html#pandas.DataFrame.values) may
involve copying data and coercing values to a common dtype, a relatively expensive
operation. [`DataFrame.to_numpy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.to_numpy.html#pandas.DataFrame.to_numpy), being a method, makes it clearer that the
returned NumPy array may not be a view on the same data in the DataFrame.

payload.content:
## Accelerated operations[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#accelerated-operations)

pandas has support for accelerating certain types of binary numerical and boolean operations using
the `numexpr` library and the `bottleneck` libraries.

These libraries are especially useful when dealing with large data sets, and provide large
speedups. `numexpr` uses smart chunking, caching, and multiple cores. `bottleneck` is
a set of specialized cython routines that are especially fast when dealing with arrays that have
`nans`.

You are highly encouraged to install both libraries. See the section
[Recommended Dependencies](https://pandas.pydata.org/getting_started/install.html#install-recommended-dependencies) for more installation info.

These are both enabled to be used by default, you can control this by setting the options:

```
pd.set_option("compute.use_bottleneck", False)
pd.set_option("compute.use_numexpr", False)
```

payload.title: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation
payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Flexible binary operations[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#flexible-binary-operations)
payload.content:
## Flexible binary operations[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#flexible-binary-operations)

With binary operations between pandas data structures, there are two key points of interest:

- Broadcasting behavior between higher- (e.g. DataFrame) and lower-dimensional (e.g. Series) objects.
- Missing data in computations.

We will demonstrate how to manage these issues independently, though they can be handled simultaneously.

payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Matching / broadcasting behavior[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#matching-broadcasting-behavior)
payload.content:
## Matching / broadcasting behavior[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#matching-broadcasting-behavior)

DataFrame has the methods [`add()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.add.html#pandas.DataFrame.add), [`sub()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sub.html#pandas.DataFrame.sub),
[`mul()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.mul.html#pandas.DataFrame.mul), [`div()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.div.html#pandas.DataFrame.div) and related functions
[`radd()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.radd.html#pandas.DataFrame.radd), [`rsub()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.rsub.html#pandas.DataFrame.rsub), …
for carrying out binary operations. For broadcasting behavior,
Series input is of primary interest. Using these functions, you can use to
either match on the *index* or *columns* via the **axis** keyword:

```
In [18]: df = pd.DataFrame(
   ....:     {
   ....:         "one": pd.Series(np.random.randn(3), index=["a", "b", "c"]),
   ....:         "two": pd.Series(np.random.randn(4), index=["a", "b", "c", "d"]),
   ....:         "three": pd.Series(np.random.randn(3), index=["b", "c", "d"]),
   ....:     }
   ....: )
   ....: 
In [19]: df
Out[19]: 
        one       two     three
a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172
In [20]: row = df.iloc[1]
In [21]: column = df["two"]
In [22]: df.sub(row, axis="columns")
Out[22]: 
        one       two     three
a  1.051928 -0.139606       NaN
b  0.000000  0.000000  0.000000
c  0.352192 -0.433754  1.277825
d       NaN -1.632779 -0.562782
In [23]: df.sub(row, axis=1)
Out[23]: 
        one       two     three

Furthermore you can align a level of a MultiIndexed DataFrame with a Series.

```
In [26]: dfmi = df.copy()

first second                              
1     a      -0.377535  0.000000       NaN
      b      -1.569069  0.000000 -1.962513

of the DataFrame (not the rows); to broadcast row-wise, pass `axis=0` to

Series and Index also support the [`divmod()`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#divmod) builtin. This function takes
the floor division and modulo operation at the same time returning a two-tuple
of the same type as the left hand side. For example:

```

payload.content:
## Missing data / operations with fill values[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#missing-data-operations-with-fill-values)

In Series and DataFrame, the arithmetic functions have the option of inputting
a *fill\_value*, namely a value to substitute when at most one of the values at
a location are missing. For example, when adding two DataFrame objects, you may
wish to treat NaN as 0 unless both DataFrames are missing that value, in which
case the result will be NaN (you can later replace NaN with some other value
using `fillna` if you wish).

```
In [42]: df2 = df.copy()
In [43]: df2.loc["a", "three"] = 1.0
In [44]: df
Out[44]: 
        one       two     three
a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172
In [45]: df2
Out[45]: 
        one       two     three
a  1.394981  1.772517  1.000000
b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172
In [46]: df + df2
Out[46]: 
        one       two     three
a  2.789963  3.545034       NaN
b  0.686107  3.824246 -0.100780
c  1.390491  2.956737  2.454870
d       NaN  0.558688 -1.226343
In [47]: df.add(df2, fill_value=0)
Out[47]: 
        one       two     three
a  2.789963  3.545034  1.000000
b  0.686107  3.824246 -0.100780
c  1.390491  2.956737  2.454870
d       NaN  0.558688 -1.226343
```

payload.content:
## Flexible comparisons[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#flexible-comparisons)

Series and DataFrame have the binary comparison methods `eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `gt`,
`le`, and `ge` whose behavior is analogous to the binary
arithmetic operations described above:

```
In [48]: df.gt(df2)
Out[48]: 
     one    two  three
a  False  False  False
b  False  False  False
c  False  False  False
d  False  False  False
In [49]: df2.ne(df)
Out[49]: 
     one    two  three
a  False  False   True
b  False  False  False
c  False  False  False
d   True  False  False
```
These operations produce a pandas object of the same type as the left-hand-side
input that is of dtype `bool`. These `boolean` objects can be used in
indexing operations, see the section on [Boolean indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/indexing.html#indexing-boolean).

payload.content:
## Boolean reductions[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#boolean-reductions)

You can apply the reductions: [`empty`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.empty.html#pandas.DataFrame.empty), [`any()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.any.html#pandas.DataFrame.any),
[`all()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.all.html#pandas.DataFrame.all).

```
In [50]: (df > 0).all()
Out[50]: 
one      False
two       True
three    False
dtype: bool
In [51]: (df > 0).any()
Out[51]: 
one      True
two      True
three    True
dtype: bool
```
You can reduce to a final boolean value.

```
In [52]: (df > 0).any().any()
Out[52]: np.True_
```
You can test if a pandas object is empty, via the [`empty`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.empty.html#pandas.DataFrame.empty) property.

```
In [53]: df.empty
Out[53]: False
In [54]: pd.DataFrame(columns=list("ABC")).empty
Out[54]: True
```
Warning

Asserting the truthiness of a pandas object will raise an error, as the testing of the emptiness or values is ambiguous.

```
In [55]: if df:
   ....:     print(True)
   ....: 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[55], line 1
----> 1 if df:
      2     print(True)
File ~/work/pandas/pandas/pandas/core/generic.py:1445, in NDFrame.__bool__(self)
   1443     @final
   1444     def __bool__(self) -> NoReturn:
-> 1445         raise ValueError(
   1446             f"The truth value of a {type(self).__name__} is ambiguous. "
   1447             "Use a.empty, a.item(), a.any() or a.all()."
   1448         )
ValueError: The truth value of a DataFrame is ambiguous. Use a.empty, a.item(), a.any() or a.all().
```

payload.content:
## Comparing if objects are equivalent[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#comparing-if-objects-are-equivalent)

Often you may find that there is more than one way to compute the same
result.  As a simple example, consider `df + df` and `df * 2`. To test
that these two computations produce the same result, given the tools
shown above, you might imagine using `(df + df == df * 2).all()`. But in
fact, this expression is False:

```
In [57]: df + df == df * 2
Out[57]: 
     one   two  three
a   True  True  False
b   True  True   True
c   True  True   True
d  False  True   True
In [58]: (df + df == df * 2).all()
Out[58]: 
one      False
two       True
three    False
dtype: bool
```
Notice that the boolean DataFrame `df + df == df * 2` contains some False values!
This is because NaNs do not compare as equals:

```
In [59]: np.nan == np.nan
Out[59]: False
```
So, NDFrames (such as Series and DataFrames)
have an [`equals()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.equals.html#pandas.DataFrame.equals) method for testing equality, with NaNs in
corresponding locations treated as equal.

```
In [60]: (df + df).equals(df * 2)
Out[60]: True
```
Note that the Series or DataFrame index needs to be in the same order for equality to be True:

```
In [61]: df1 = pd.DataFrame({"col": ["foo", 0, np.nan]})
In [62]: df2 = pd.DataFrame({"col": [np.nan, 0, "foo"]}, index=[2, 1, 0])
In [63]: df1.equals(df2)
Out[63]: False
In [64]: df1.equals(df2.sort_index())
Out[64]: True
```

payload.content:
## Comparing array-like objects[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#comparing-array-like-objects)

You can conveniently perform element-wise comparisons when comparing a pandas data structure with a scalar value:

```
In [65]: pd.Series(["foo", "bar", "baz"]) == "foo"
Out[65]: 
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
In [66]: pd.Index(["foo", "bar", "baz"]) == "foo"
Out[66]: array([ True, False, False])
```
pandas also handles element-wise comparisons between different array-like objects of the same length:

```
In [67]: pd.Series(["foo", "bar", "baz"]) == pd.Index(["foo", "bar", "qux"])
Out[67]: 
0     True
1     True
2    False
dtype: bool
In [68]: pd.Series(["foo", "bar", "baz"]) == np.array(["foo", "bar", "qux"])
Out[68]: 
0     True
1     True
2    False
dtype: bool
```

raise a ValueError:

payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Combining overlapping data sets[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#combining-overlapping-data-sets)
payload.content:
## Combining overlapping data sets[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#combining-overlapping-data-sets)

A problem occasionally arising is the combination of two similar data sets
where values in one are preferred over the other. An example would be two data
series representing a particular economic indicator where one is considered to
be of “higher quality”. However, the lower quality series might extend further
back in history or have more complete data coverage. As such, we would like to
combine two DataFrame objects where missing values in one DataFrame are
conditionally filled with like-labeled values from the other DataFrame. The
function implementing this operation is [`combine_first()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.combine_first.html#pandas.DataFrame.combine_first),
which we illustrate:

```
In [71]: df1 = pd.DataFrame(
   ....:     {"A": [1.0, np.nan, 3.0, 5.0, np.nan], "B": [np.nan, 2.0, 3.0, np.nan, 6.0]}
   ....: )
   ....: 
In [72]: df2 = pd.DataFrame(
   ....:     {
   ....:         "A": [5.0, 2.0, 4.0, np.nan, 3.0, 7.0],
   ....:         "B": [np.nan, np.nan, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0],
   ....:     }
   ....: )
   ....: 
In [73]: df1
Out[73]: 
     A    B
0  1.0  NaN
1  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  3.0
3  5.0  NaN
4  NaN  6.0
In [74]: df2
Out[74]: 
     A    B
0  5.0  NaN
1  2.0  NaN
2  4.0  3.0
3  NaN  4.0
4  3.0  6.0
5  7.0  8.0
In [75]: df1.combine_first(df2)
Out[75]: 
     A    B
0  1.0  NaN
1  2.0  2.0
2  3.0  3.0
3  5.0  4.0
4  3.0  6.0
5  7.0  8.0
```

payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > General DataFrame combine[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#general-dataframe-combine)
payload.content:
## General DataFrame combine[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#general-dataframe-combine)

The [`combine_first()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.combine_first.html#pandas.DataFrame.combine_first) method above calls the more general
[`DataFrame.combine()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.combine.html#pandas.DataFrame.combine). This method takes another DataFrame
and a combiner function, aligns the input DataFrame and then passes the combiner
function pairs of Series (i.e., columns whose names are the same).

So, for instance, to reproduce [`combine_first()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.combine_first.html#pandas.DataFrame.combine_first) as above:

```
In [76]: def combiner(x, y):
   ....:     return np.where(pd.isna(x), y, x)
   ....: 
In [77]: df1.combine(df2, combiner)
Out[77]: 
     A    B
0  1.0  NaN
1  2.0  2.0
2  3.0  3.0
3  5.0  4.0
4  3.0  6.0
5  7.0  8.0
```

payload.breadcrumb: Essential basic functionality — pandas 3.1.0 documentation > Essential basic functionality[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#essential-basic-functionality) > Descriptive statistics[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#descriptive-statistics)
payload.content:
## Descriptive statistics[#](https://pandas.pydata.org#descriptive-statistics)

There exists a large number of methods for computing descriptive statistics and
other related operations on [Series](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/series.html#api-series-stats), [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/frame.html#api-dataframe-stats). Most of these
are aggregations (hence producing a lower-dimensional result) like
[`sum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sum.html#pandas.DataFrame.sum), [`mean()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.mean.html#pandas.DataFrame.mean), and [`quantile()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.quantile.html#pandas.DataFrame.quantile),
but some of them, like [`cumsum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.cumsum.html#pandas.DataFrame.cumsum) and [`cumprod()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.cumprod.html#pandas.DataFrame.cumprod),
produce an object of the same size. Generally speaking, these methods take an
**axis** argument, just like *ndarray.{sum, std, …}*, but the axis can be
specified by name or integer:

- **Series**: no axis argument needed
- **DataFrame**: “index” (axis=0, default), “columns” (axis=1)

For example:

```
In [78]: df
Out[78]: 
        one       two     three
a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
b  0.343054  1.912123 -0.050390
c  0.695246  1.478369  1.227435
d       NaN  0.279344 -0.613172
In [79]: df.mean(axis=0)
Out[79]: 
one      0.811094
two      1.360588
three    0.187958
dtype: float64
In [80]: df.mean(axis=1)
Out[80]: 
a    1.583749
b    0.734929
c    1.133683
d   -0.166914
dtype: float64
```
All such methods have a `skipna` option signaling whether to exclude missing
data (`True` by default):

```

payload.content:
three    0.187958
dtype: float64
In [80]: df.mean(axis=1)
Out[80]: 
a    1.583749
b    0.734929

All such methods have a `skipna` option signaling whether to exclude missing
data (`True` by default):

```
In [81]: df.sum(axis=0, skipna=False)
Out[81]: 
one           NaN
two      5.442353
three         NaN
dtype: float64
In [82]: df.sum(axis=1, skipna=True)
Out[82]: 
a    3.167498
b    2.204786
c    3.401050
d   -0.333828
dtype: float64
```
Combined with the broadcasting / arithmetic behavior, one can describe various statistical procedures, like standardization (rendering data zero mean and standard deviation of 1), very concisely:

```
In [83]: ts_stand = (df - df.mean()) / df.std()
In [84]: ts_stand.std()
Out[84]: 
one      1.0
two      1.0
three    1.0
dtype: float64
In [85]: xs_stand = df.sub(df.mean(axis=1), axis=0).div(df.std(axis=1), axis=0)
In [86]: xs_stand.std(axis=1)
Out[86]: 
a    1.0
b    1.0
c    1.0
d    1.0
dtype: float64
```
Note that methods like [`cumsum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.cumsum.html#pandas.DataFrame.cumsum) and [`cumprod()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.cumprod.html#pandas.DataFrame.cumprod)
preserve the location of `NaN` values. This is somewhat different from
[`expanding()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.expanding.html#pandas.DataFrame.expanding) and [`rolling()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.rolling.html#pandas.DataFrame.rolling) since `NaN` behavior
is furthermore dictated by a `min_periods` parameter.

```
In [87]: df.cumsum()
Out[87]: 
        one       two     three
a  1.394981  1.772517       NaN
b  1.738035  3.684640 -0.050390
c  2.433281  5.163008  1.177045
